=== Installation.md ===

sidebar_position: 2

# Installation

```
bun install -g @harmoniclabs/pebble-cli
```

:::info `bun` or `npm`

We suggest using `bun` for installation if you have it available on your machine.

This is because [`bun`](https://bun.sh/) offers some good performance improvements for the compiler.

Alternatively, if you don't want to use `bun`, you can use any javascript package manager of your choice, since the source of the compiler is present on the npm public registry.

`npm` is the package manager use by `NodeJS`.
Most of the times you'll find `npm` already present on your machine.

If that is not the case, you can install `node` and `npm` from the [`NodeJS` website](https://nodejs.org/en/)

:::

### executable from source

:::warning `bun` required

Building an executable assumes `bun` is present on your machine

:::

```
git clone https://github.com/HarmonicLabs/pebble
cd pebble/packages/pebble-cli
npm i # install dependencies
npm run build-exe
```

:::info `pebble` executable

if the build was successful, you should see an executable at the `out/pebble` path.

:::

## Editor support — `Pebble Language` extension

The official VS Code extension ships syntax highlighting, on-save type checking, and Language-Server-Protocol features (go-to-definition, hover types, diagnostics) for `.pebble` files.

### From inside VS Code

1. Open the Extensions view: `Ctrl+Shift+X` (or `Cmd+Shift+X` on macOS).
2. Search for **`Pebble Language`**.
3. Install the entry published by `HarmonicLabs`.

### From the command line

```bash
code --install-extension HarmonicLabs.pebble-lsp
```

Or, for VS Codium / OSS builds that use the Open VSX registry:

```bash
codium --install-extension HarmonicLabs.pebble-lsp
```

### Marketplace links

- VS Code Marketplace: [`HarmonicLabs.pebble-lsp`](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=HarmonicLabs.pebble-lsp)
- Open VSX (VS Codium, Cursor, etc.): [`HarmonicLabs/pebble-lsp`](https://open-vsx.org/extension/HarmonicLabs/pebble-lsp)

:::info `pebble` on `PATH` recommended

The extension's LSP shells out to the `pebble` CLI for compilation diagnostics. Install it first (see the section at the top of this page) so the editor can drive real type-checks rather than just colourise the file.

:::

## Sanity check

If everything proceeded smoothly, you should have the `pebble` command available in your terminal.

You can make sure everything is working properly by running

```bash
pebble --version
```

which should output something like

```text
pebble-cli version:      0.6.0
pebble language version: 0.6.0
commit hash:             4374aea5e466396ce524dcf7dffa348adf7c75f9
```

you can also run

```bash
pebble help
```

for more info on the commands, or

```bash
pebble repl
```

to start an interactive session in the project of the working directory — see [CLI](./onchain/CLI.md#repl).

:::info Node.js 22 or newer
The CLI declares `"engines": { "node": ">=22", "bun": ">=1.2.0" }`.
:::

=== Project Setup.md ===

sidebar_position: 3

# Project Setup

you can create a new pebble project by simply running
```bash
pebble init
```

The program will then ask a few question, and generate a new repository.

`pebble init` generates a `pebble.config.json` — see [Compiler Configuration](./onchain/Compiler%20Configuration.md) for the full schema.

In your new repository you can run 
```bash
pebble compile
```

to generate the contract uplc.

Once you have tests in your project, run them with `pebble test` — see [Testing](./onchain/Testing.md).

## Examples

Have a look at [Examples](./category/examples) for some example project

=== Welcome to Pebble.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 1
sidebar_label: Welcome to Pebble

# Pebble

Built with ❤️ by [Harmonic Laboratories](https://www.harmoniclabs.tech/)

This documentation is for `pebble`. Feel free to ask for help in the [Harmonic Labs' discord server](https://discord.gg/CGKNcG7ade)

## Introduction

Pebble is a **strongly-typed domain-specific language (DSL)** for writing **Cardano smart contracts**. A simple, yet rock solid, functional language with an imperative bias, targeting UPLC.

import RunnableExample from '@site/src/components/RunnableExample';

<RunnableExample
initialCode={`const n = 10;\n\nlet result = 0;\nfor( let i = 0; i <= n; i++ ) {\n    result += i;\n}\n\n/*\ntrace result;\n/*/\nassert result === 55 else "boom";\n//*/`}
height="250px"
/>

At its heart, Pebble is:

- A **language**: with its own parser, type checker, and compiler.  
- A **toolchain**: including a CLI, compiler, and integrations for DApp workflows.  
- A **bridge**: between human-readable smart contract code and low-level Plutus Core.  

Pebble is **statement-oriented** (with constructs like `let`, `if`, `while`, `match`, `return`), but under the hood, **everything still compiles down to Plutus Core expressions**, maintaining full functional correctness.  

This makes Pebble feel familiar for developers coming from JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, or Solidity, while retaining the strict guarantees of Plutus.

To sum it all up, `pebble` is a first-class language with its own syntax and compiler, but still exposes onchain/offchain type ecosystems for contract and DApp integrations.

# Getting started

See [Installation](./Installation) to begin your journey in pebble

## Why Pebble?

Cardano contracts require precision, and writing them directly in Plutus Core or Haskell is error-prone.  

Pebble takes the next step:  

- **Readable syntax** → close to common c-like programming languages  
- **Composable abstractions** → structs, options, pattern matching  
- **Direct blockchain access** → via on-chain types (Tx, ScriptContext, PubKeyHash, etc.)  
- **Modern tooling** → integrated CLI, compilation, and test workflows  

=== examples/Hello World.md ===

---
sidebar_position: 0
---

# Hello World

The smallest useful Pebble contract: a script that locks a UTxO until the owner signs a transaction that includes a fixed greeting in the redeemer. It exercises the `contract`/`state` machinery, signature-checking, and a redeemer payload — everything the larger examples build on.

## On-chain: `hello_world.pebble`

```ts
contract HelloWorld
{
    state Locked {
        owner: PubKeyHash

        spend greet(message: bytes)
        {
            const { tx, state: { owner } } = context;
            assert tx.requiredSigners.includes(owner);
            assert message == "Hello pebble"; // double-quoted literals are bytes (utf-8)
        }
    }
}
```

### Why this shape

- **One `state` constructor**, so the datum is `Locked{ owner }` — a single CBOR `Constr(0, [B owner])`.
- **The redeemer is `(message: bytes)`** — the method's parameters become the redeemer at the call site.
- **The script aborts** if the message doesn't match exactly. See [Failures](../onchain/reference/Failures.md).

## Off-chain: TypeScript with `@harmoniclabs/buildooor`

```ts
import {
    Address, Credential, Hash28,
    DataConstr, DataB,
    TxBuilder, TxOut,
} from "@harmoniclabs/buildooor";
import { readFile } from "fs/promises";
import { provider } from "./provider";

const scriptCbor = await readFile("./hello_world.uplc");
const helloHash  = new Hash28(/* blake2b_224(scriptCbor) */);
const helloAddr  = new Address("mainnet", Credential.script(helloHash));
```

### Lock

```ts
async function lock({ ownerPkh, lockValue, wallet, privateKey }) {
    // Constr(0, [B ownerPkh]) — single-constructor sum for state `Locked`
    const datum = new DataConstr(0, [ new DataB(ownerPkh.toBuffer()) ]);

    const txBuilder = new TxBuilder(await provider.getProtocolParameters());

    const tx = txBuilder.buildSync({
        inputs: wallet.utxos.map((utxo) => ({ utxo })),
        outputs: [
            new TxOut({
                address: helloAddr,
                value:   lockValue,
                datum,
            }),
        ],
        changeAddress: wallet.address,
    });
    tx.signWith(privateKey);
    return await provider.submitTx(tx);
}
```

### Greet (unlock)

```ts
async function greet({ lockedUtxo, ownerWallet, ownerPrivateKey, scriptRefUtxo }) {
    const txBuilder = new TxBuilder(await provider.getProtocolParameters());

    const message  = new TextEncoder().encode("Hello pebble");
    const redeemer = new DataConstr(0, [ new DataB(message) ]);  // greet(bytes)

    const tx = txBuilder.buildSync({
        inputs: [
            {
                utxo: lockedUtxo,
                referenceScript: { refUtxo: scriptRefUtxo, redeemer },
            },
            ...ownerWallet.utxos.map((utxo) => ({ utxo })),
        ],
        outputs: [
            new TxOut({
                address: ownerWallet.address,
                value:   lockedUtxo.resolved.value,
            }),
        ],
        collaterals:     [ ownerWallet.utxos[0] ],
        changeAddress:   ownerWallet.address,
        requiredSigners: [ ownerWallet.pkh ],  // satisfies tx.requiredSigners.includes(owner)
    });
    tx.signWith(ownerPrivateKey);
    return await provider.submitTx(tx);
}
```

## Uses

- [`contract`](../onchain/Contract%20Statements.md), [`state`](../onchain/State.md), [`spend`](../onchain/concepts/Validators%20101.md)
- [`assert`](../onchain/Syntax/Control%20Flow%20Statements.md), `tx.requiredSigners.includes(...)`
- [`string.toBytes`](../onchain/Prelude/String.mdx), `bytes` equality via `==`
- buildooor: `TxBuilder.buildSync`, `DataConstr`, `DataB`, `Credential.script`

## See also

- [Validators 101](../onchain/concepts/Validators%20101.md) — `context` shape and script-purpose dispatch
- [State](../onchain/State.md) — the keyword used for the datum
- [Simple Order Book DEX](./Simple%20order%20book%20DEX.md) — same patterns at protocol scale


=== examples/Simple minting policy.md ===

---
sidebar_position: 1
---

# Simple minting policy

A native token's supply is controlled by its **minting policy** — a Plutus script invoked under the `Mint` purpose whenever tokens with that policy's hash are minted or burned. This example shows two policies that illustrate the spectrum:

1. **AllowAnyMint** — a permissive policy that accepts every mint and burn. Useful as a teaching example, never in production.
2. **OneShot** — a tightly-constrained policy that can only mint a fixed token name **once**, by requiring a specific UTxO to be consumed in the same transaction. This pattern is how NFTs get their uniqueness on Cardano.

## On-chain

### AllowAnyMint

```ts
contract AllowAnyMint
{
    mint allowAnything() {}
}
```

The body is empty: no `assert`, no `fail`, so the script always succeeds. Anyone with this policy hash can mint or burn arbitrary amounts.

### OneShot (parameterised by a UTxO ref)

```ts
contract OneShot
{
    param seedRef: TxOutRef;
    param tokenName: TokenName;

    mint mintOnce()
    {
        const { tx, policy: ownPolicy } = context;

        // 1. The "seed" UTxO must be one of the transaction's inputs.
        //    Once it's spent, the same transaction can never be replayed,
        //    so the mint can never happen again.
        assert tx.inputs.some((i) => i.ref == this.seedRef);

        // 2. EXACT mint: this policy, our token name, amount = 1 — and
        //    nothing else (defends against minting an extra side-token in
        //    the same tx). Values are canonically normalized, so data
        //    equality is order-independent.
        const expectedMint = std.value.zero
            .insert( ownPolicy, this.tokenName, 1 );
        assert tx.mint.toData() == expectedMint.toData();
    }
}
```

### Why this shape

- **`OneShot(seedRef, tokenName)` takes contract parameters.** At compile time you bake in the specific UTxO that gates the mint; the resulting validator has a unique policy hash. See [Contract Statements](../onchain/Contract%20Statements.md).
- **`policy` carries the policy ID** in a `mint` method's `context`. Contract `param`s are read through `this.` (`this.seedRef`, `this.tokenName`).
- **Both checks together** (input present + exactly one mint entry) make this an **NFT primitive**: minting can happen at most once, and only the named token is created.

## Off-chain: TypeScript with `@harmoniclabs/buildooor`

```ts
import {
    Address, Credential, Hash28, Value,
    DataConstr, DataB, DataI,
    TxBuilder, TxOut, UTxO,
} from "@harmoniclabs/buildooor";
import { readFile } from "fs/promises";
import { provider } from "./provider";
```

### Mint under `OneShot`

```ts
async function mintOneShot({
    oneShotScriptCbor,        // Uint8Array — compiled with the seedRef + tokenName baked in
    oneShotPolicyHash,        // Hash28 of the script above
    tokenName,                // Uint8Array
    seedUtxo,                 // UTxO matching the seedRef baked into the script
    receiverAddress,          // Address — who gets the freshly minted token
    minterWallet,             // { address, utxos }
    minterPrivateKey,
}) {
    const txBuilder = new TxBuilder(await provider.getProtocolParameters());

    // mintOnce() takes no arguments — redeemer is Constr(0, []).
    const redeemer = new DataConstr(0, []);

    // The freshly minted token, paid to the receiver.
    const mintedToken = Value.singleAsset(oneShotPolicyHash, tokenName, 1n);

    const tx = txBuilder.buildSync({
        inputs: [
            { utxo: seedUtxo },                    // <- satisfies the seedRef check
            ...minterWallet.utxos.map((utxo) => ({ utxo })),
        ],
        mints: [
            {
                value:  mintedToken,
                script: {
                    inline: oneShotScriptCbor,
                    redeemer,
                },
            },
        ],
        outputs: [
            new TxOut({
                address: receiverAddress,
                // The output must carry the minted token plus enough ADA
                // to meet the protocol's min-UTxO requirement.
                value:   Value.merge(
                    mintedToken,
                    Value.lovelaces(1_500_000n),
                ),
            }),
        ],
        collaterals:   [ minterWallet.utxos[0] ],
        changeAddress: minterWallet.address,
    });
    tx.signWith(minterPrivateKey);
    return await provider.submitTx(tx);
}
```

### Burn (sketch)

To burn, mint a **negative** quantity. The policy script runs the same `mintOnce()` body, so an `OneShot` script can't burn — only the looser `AllowAnyMint` can. A more realistic production policy adds a `mint burn()` method that checks the burner's signature and that the burn quantity is negative.

## Uses

- [`contract`](../onchain/Contract%20Statements.md) with parameters, `mint` method-kind
- `purpose` destructuring via [`Mint{ policyId }`](../onchain/API/types/ScriptContext/ScriptPurpose.md)
- [`List<T>.some`](../onchain/Prelude/List.mdx), [`Value.amountOf`](../onchain/Prelude/Value.mdx)
- [`Optional`](../onchain/Prelude/Optional.mdx) match on a `LinearMap.lookup` result
- buildooor: `mints` field of `buildSync`, `Value.singleAsset`, `Value.merge`, `Value.lovelaces`

## See also

- [Validators 101](../onchain/concepts/Validators%20101.md) — how `purpose` is bound for a `mint` script
- [Failures](../onchain/reference/Failures.md) — when destructuring `Mint{ ... }` can fail
- [Pitfalls](../onchain/reference/Pitfalls.md) — minting more than you intended


=== examples/Simple order book DEX.md ===

---
sidebar_position: 4
---

# Simple Order Book DEX

A worked example of a single-asset order book on Cardano. Each order is its own UTxO at the contract's address; a counterparty fills an order by spending it and paying the owner the agreed amount. Cancellation is permitted by the owner.

The on-chain code uses the **`contract`** and **`state`** keywords introduced in Pebble v0.3.0. The off-chain code uses **[`@harmoniclabs/buildooor`](https://github.com/HarmonicLabs/buildooor)** to construct and submit transactions.

## What we're building

Three actions on each order UTxO:

1. **Place** — wallet creates an output at the contract address, datum = the order's terms.
2. **Fill** — anyone spends the order, sending the requested payment to the order's owner.
3. **Cancel** — the owner spends the order back to themselves.

The contract has a single `state` (`Simple`) whose fields capture the order's terms. The `spend fill(...)` method enforces the fill rules; a second `spend cancelOrder()` method on the same state handles cancellation.

## On-chain: `simple_order_book.pebble`

```ts
contract SimpleOrderBook
{
    state Simple {
        // hash that's allowed to cancel and that receives the payment on fill
        ownerHash: bytes
        // token to be paid in
        policy: PolicyId
        tokenName: TokenName
        // minimum amount of (policy, tokenName) the owner must receive
        minReceiveAmount: int

        spend fill(inputIdx: int, outputIdx: int)
        {
            const {
                tx,
                spendingRef: purposeRef,
                state: { ownerHash, policy, tokenName, minReceiveAmount }
            } = context;

            // The input named in the redeemer is this script's invocation
            const { ref: inputRef, resolved: spendingInput } =
                tx.inputs[inputIdx];
            assert purposeRef == inputRef;

            const ownAddr = spendingInput.address;
            const ownScriptHash = ownAddr.payment.hash();

            // Prevent double satisfaction: at most one of *this script's*
            // UTxOs may be spent in the same transaction.
            const ownInputs = tx.inputs.filter(
                (i) => i.resolved.address.payment.hash() == ownScriptHash
            );
            assert ownInputs.length() == 1;

            // The named output must pay the owner the agreed token amount,
            // routed to an address that pays to `ownerHash`.
            const userOutput = tx.outputs[outputIdx];
            assert userOutput.address.payment.hash() == ownerHash;
            assert userOutput.value.amountOf(policy, tokenName) >= minReceiveAmount;
        }

        spend cancelOrder()
        {
            const { tx, state: { ownerHash } } = context;
            assert tx.requiredSigners.includes(ownerHash);
        }
    }
}
```

### Why this shape

- **`state Simple { ... }`** declares a datum type. The compiler synthesizes a sum-type with one constructor for `Simple`; the order's UTxO carries a CBOR-encoded `Simple{ ownerHash, policy, tokenName, minReceiveAmount }` as its datum.
- **`spend fill` inside the state** binds `state` automatically — every state field is in scope after destructuring `context`.
- **`spend cancelOrder` on the same state** is the cancellation path; the redeemer selects which method runs. See [Contract Statements](../onchain/Contract%20Statements.md) for the dispatch rules.
- **Double-satisfaction defence**: `tx.inputs.filter(...).length() == 1` ensures one fill output can't satisfy two orders. See [Pitfalls — Double-satisfaction](../onchain/reference/Pitfalls.md).

## Off-chain: TypeScript with `@harmoniclabs/buildooor`

```ts
import {
    Address, Credential, Hash28, Value,
    DataConstr, DataB, DataI,
    TxBuilder, TxOut, UTxO,
} from "@harmoniclabs/buildooor";
import { readFile } from "fs/promises";
// Your provider — Blockfrost, Koios, Maestro, Ogmios, ...
import { provider } from "./provider";

// The compiled contract: load `simple_order_book.uplc` as a Cardano script
const scriptCbor = await readFile("./simple_order_book.uplc");
const orderBookScript = /* parse scriptCbor to a Cardano Script value */;
const orderBookHash   = new Hash28(/* blake2b_224(scriptCbor) */);
const orderBookAddr   = new Address(
    "mainnet",
    Credential.script(orderBookHash)
);
```

### 1. Placing an order

Build a UTxO at `orderBookAddr` whose datum encodes a `Simple{ ... }` state:

```ts
async function placeOrder({
    ownerPkh,            // Hash28
    payPolicy,           // Hash28 (a Cardano script hash)
    payTokenName,        // Uint8Array
    minReceive,          // bigint
    lockValue,           // Value — what the order itself contains
    wallet,              // { address, utxos }
    privateKey,
}) {
    // The state datum: a single-constructor sum, hence Constr(0, [...])
    const orderDatum = new DataConstr(0, [
        new DataB(ownerPkh.toBuffer()),
        new DataB(payPolicy.toBuffer()),
        new DataB(payTokenName),
        new DataI(minReceive),
    ]);

    const txBuilder = new TxBuilder(await provider.getProtocolParameters());

    const tx = txBuilder.buildSync({
        inputs: wallet.utxos.map((utxo) => ({ utxo })),
        outputs: [
            new TxOut({
                address: orderBookAddr,
                value:   lockValue,
                datum:   orderDatum,
            }),
        ],
        changeAddress: wallet.address,
    });

    tx.signWith(privateKey);
    return await provider.submitTx(tx);
}
```

### 2. Filling an order

The filler spends the order UTxO with the `fill` redeemer (`inputIdx` of the order in `tx.inputs`, `outputIdx` of the payment in `tx.outputs`), pays the owner the agreed amount, and keeps the locked value.

```ts
async function fillOrder({
    orderUtxo,           // UTxO at orderBookAddr
    orderState,          // { ownerHash, policy, tokenName, minReceiveAmount }
    fillerWallet,        // { address, utxos }
    privateKey,
    scriptRefUtxo,       // UTxO carrying the orderBook script as reference
}) {
    const txBuilder = new TxBuilder(await provider.getProtocolParameters());

    // Build the predicted input/output order so we can quote indices in the
    // redeemer. buildooor preserves the order you provide.
    const orderInput = {
        utxo: orderUtxo,
        referenceScript: {
            refUtxo:  scriptRefUtxo,
            redeemer: new DataConstr(0, [   // Constr(0, [...]) = `fill(...)`
                new DataI(0),               // inputIdx: position of orderUtxo
                new DataI(0),               // outputIdx: position of payment
            ]),
        },
    };

    const paymentOutput = new TxOut({
        address: Address.fromCredentials(
            "mainnet",
            Credential.keyHash(orderState.ownerHash),
        ),
        value: Value.singleAsset(
            new Hash28(orderState.policy),
            orderState.tokenName,
            BigInt(orderState.minReceiveAmount),
        ),
    });

    // The filler also keeps whatever was locked in the order, minus the
    // payment they had to source from their own UTxOs.
    const lockedKeptByFiller = new TxOut({
        address: fillerWallet.address,
        value:   orderUtxo.resolved.value,
    });

    const tx = txBuilder.buildSync({
        inputs:  [ orderInput, ...fillerWallet.utxos.map((utxo) => ({ utxo })) ],
        outputs: [ paymentOutput, lockedKeptByFiller ],
        collaterals:   [ fillerWallet.utxos[0] ],
        changeAddress: fillerWallet.address,
    });

    tx.signWith(privateKey);
    return await provider.submitTx(tx);
}
```

### 3. Cancelling an order

The owner spends the order back to themselves under the `cancelOrder` purpose:

```ts
async function cancelOrder({
    orderUtxo,
    ownerWallet,        // { address, utxos, pkh } — must be the order's owner
    ownerPrivateKey,
    scriptRefUtxo,
}) {
    const txBuilder = new TxBuilder(await provider.getProtocolParameters());

    const orderInput = {
        utxo: orderUtxo,
        referenceScript: {
            refUtxo:  scriptRefUtxo,
            // Constr(1, []) selects the second `spend` method (`cancelOrder`)
            // since `fill` is Constr(0, [...]).
            redeemer: new DataConstr(1, []),
        },
    };

    const tx = txBuilder.buildSync({
        inputs: [ orderInput, ...ownerWallet.utxos.map((utxo) => ({ utxo })) ],
        outputs: [
            new TxOut({
                address: ownerWallet.address,
                value:   orderUtxo.resolved.value,
            }),
        ],
        collaterals:        [ ownerWallet.utxos[0] ],
        changeAddress:      ownerWallet.address,
        requiredSigners:    [ ownerWallet.pkh ],   // satisfies `tx.requiredSigners.includes(ownerHash)`
    });

    tx.signWith(ownerPrivateKey);
    return await provider.submitTx(tx);
}
```

---

# Vesting

A vesting contract locks funds until a beneficiary becomes eligible to claim them after a deadline (POSIX time). Two parties, two phases:

1. **Lock** — the depositor pays funds to the contract address with a datum naming the `beneficiary` and the `deadline`.
2. **Unlock** — after `deadline`, the beneficiary spends the UTxO. Before `deadline`, every unlock attempt aborts.

The on-chain logic checks the transaction's validity-interval lower bound against `deadline`, plus the beneficiary's signature.

## On-chain: `vesting.pebble`

```ts
contract Vesting
{
    state Locked {
        beneficiary: PubKeyHash
        deadline: int                    // POSIX milliseconds

        spend claim()
        {
            const { tx, state: { beneficiary, deadline } } = context;

            assert tx.requiredSigners.includes(beneficiary);

            // tx.validityInterval.from.boundary is the earliest the tx is
            // allowed to be on-chain. If the lower bound is >= deadline,
            // we *know* the deadline has passed when this script runs.
            const Finite{ n: txEarliest } = tx.validityInterval.from.boundary;
            assert txEarliest >= deadline;
        }
    }
}
```

### Why this shape

- **Validity-interval check, not "now"**. There is no "now" inside a validator — scripts are deterministic. Instead, the transaction promises an interval during which it's valid, and the script reads that interval. The off-chain builder picks the bound.
- **`Finite` destructuring** asserts the bound is concrete (not `-∞`). If a malicious submitter set the bound to negative infinity, the destructure would fail. See [Pitfalls](../onchain/reference/Pitfalls.md).
- **One state**, so the datum is `Locked{ beneficiary, deadline }` — `Constr(0, [B, I])`.

## Off-chain: TypeScript with `@harmoniclabs/buildooor`

```ts
import {
    Address, Credential, Hash28,
    DataConstr, DataB, DataI,
    TxBuilder, TxOut,
} from "@harmoniclabs/buildooor";
import { readFile } from "fs/promises";
import { provider } from "./provider";

const scriptCbor = await readFile("./vesting.uplc");
const vestingHash = new Hash28(/* blake2b_224(scriptCbor) */);
const vestingAddr = new Address("mainnet", Credential.script(vestingHash));
```

### Lock

```ts
async function lockVesting({
    beneficiaryPkh,   // Hash28
    deadlineMillis,   // bigint (POSIX ms)
    lockValue,        // Value
    wallet,
    privateKey,
}) {
    const datum = new DataConstr(0, [
        new DataB(beneficiaryPkh.toBuffer()),
        new DataI(deadlineMillis),
    ]);

    const txBuilder = new TxBuilder(await provider.getProtocolParameters());

    const tx = txBuilder.buildSync({
        inputs: wallet.utxos.map((utxo) => ({ utxo })),
        outputs: [
            new TxOut({
                address: vestingAddr,
                value:   lockValue,
                datum,
            }),
        ],
        changeAddress: wallet.address,
    });
    tx.signWith(privateKey);
    return await provider.submitTx(tx);
}
```

### Claim (after the deadline)

```ts
async function claimVesting({
    vestingUtxo,
    deadlineMillis,
    beneficiaryWallet,
    beneficiaryPrivateKey,
    scriptRefUtxo,
}) {
    const txBuilder = new TxBuilder(await provider.getProtocolParameters());

    // claim() takes no arguments, so its redeemer is Constr(0, []).
    const redeemer = new DataConstr(0, []);

    // Set the transaction's validity *lower bound* at or after the deadline.
    // buildooor exposes posixToSlot for this — pass `deadlineMillis` and the
    // builder picks the right slot.
    const invalidBefore = txBuilder.posixToSlot(Number(deadlineMillis));

    const tx = txBuilder.buildSync({
        inputs: [
            {
                utxo: vestingUtxo,
                referenceScript: { refUtxo: scriptRefUtxo, redeemer },
            },
            ...beneficiaryWallet.utxos.map((utxo) => ({ utxo })),
        ],
        outputs: [
            new TxOut({
                address: beneficiaryWallet.address,
                value:   vestingUtxo.resolved.value,
            }),
        ],
        collaterals:     [ beneficiaryWallet.utxos[0] ],
        changeAddress:   beneficiaryWallet.address,
        requiredSigners: [ beneficiaryWallet.pkh ],
        invalidBefore,                    // sets tx.validityInterval.from
    });
    tx.signWith(beneficiaryPrivateKey);
    return await provider.submitTx(tx);
}
```

## Uses

- [`contract`](../onchain/Contract%20Statements.md), [`state`](../onchain/State.md), `spend`
- [`Finite`](../onchain/API/types/Interval/IntervalBoundary.md), [`Interval`](../onchain/API/types/Interval/Interval.md), `tx.validityInterval`
- `tx.requiredSigners`
- buildooor: `TxBuilder.posixToSlot`, `invalidBefore`, `DataConstr`, `DataB`, `DataI`

## See also

- [Validators 101](../onchain/concepts/Validators%20101.md) — why we use the validity interval instead of a "now"
- [Pitfalls](../onchain/reference/Pitfalls.md) — destructuring an interval boundary safely
- [Hello World](./Hello%20World.md) — the same pattern without the time check

=== onchain/Builtin Interfaces.md ===

---
sidebar_position: 8
sidebar_label: Builtin Interfaces
---

# Builtin Interfaces

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

Pebble's type-class machinery is exposed via **interfaces** — sets of methods a type can implement. Two are built into the prelude and auto-derived for every type that supports them. User-defined interfaces use the same dispatch mechanism but require explicit `implements` blocks.

```ts
type Foo implements Show {
    show( self ): bytes {
        return "Foo";
    }
}
```

The compiler resolves interface methods at **monomorphisation time** — when a generic function constrained on `T: SomeInterface` is called with a concrete type, the compiler looks up that type's impl (either user-defined or built-in factory) and inlines the right method IR. There is no on-chain dictionary-passing overhead.

## `ToData`

Defines the canonical conversion of a value to Plutus `data`. Every concrete Pebble type that can be encoded as `data` automatically has a `ToData` impl — primitives, `List<T>`, `Array<T>`, `LinearMap<K, V>` (when K and V are themselves `ToData`), `Optional<T>`, structs and enums, and the native `Value`.

```ts
interface ToData {
    toData( self ): data;
}
```

The auto-derivation is provided by the compiler's built-in factory in [`populateBuiltinInterfaces.ts`](https://github.com/HarmonicLabs/pebble/blob/main/packages/pebble/src/compiler/tir/program/stdScope/populateBuiltinInterfaces.ts). For each concrete type, the factory returns the IR closure that performs the right encoding:

| Type             | Lowering                                                      |
|------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| `int`            | `iData`                                                       |
| `bytes`          | `bData`                                                       |
| `bool`           | `Constr(0/1, [])`                                             |
| `List<T>`        | `listData(map(toData<T>, xs))`                                |
| `LinearMap<K,V>` | `mapData` with `mkPairData` + `toData<K>`/`toData<V>`         |
| `Optional<T>`    | `Constr(0, [toData<T>(x)])` for `Some`, `Constr(1, [])` for `None` |
| struct           | `Constr(0, [toData(field_1), toData(field_2), ...])`          |
| enum / SoP       | `Constr(variantIndex, [toData(field_1), ...])`                |
| native `Value`   | the `valueData` builtin                                       |

### Calling it

Every value has a `.toData()` method:

```ts
const n: int = 42;
const d: data = n.toData();   // iData(42)

const xs: List<int> = [1, 2, 3];
const dl: data = xs.toData(); // listData([iData(1), iData(2), iData(3)])
```

### Implementing it on your own type

Most user types don't need a hand-rolled `ToData` — the auto-derivation covers them. Reach for an explicit impl only when you need a non-canonical encoding (e.g. a legacy on-chain shape from a previous protocol version).

```ts
struct LegacyRecord {
    a: int,
    b: bytes,
}

type LegacyRecord implements ToData {
    toData( self ): data {
        // Hand-rolled to match an older protocol's wire format.
        return std.builtins.constrData(7, [
            self.b.toData(),   // legacy order: b first, then a
            self.a.toData(),
        ]);
    }
}
```

### Using it as a constraint

Stdlib generics that need to encode `T` use a `T: ToData` constraint. `std.linearMap.prepend` is the canonical example:

```ts
// signature:  prepend<K: ToData, V: ToData>(k: K, v: V, m: LinearMap<K, V>): LinearMap<K, V>
const m: LinearMap<bytes, int> = {};
const m2 = std.linearMap.prepend(#01, 100, m);
```

## `Show`

Defines a human-readable byte representation. Built-in for primitives; user-overridable.

```ts
interface Show {
    show( self ): bytes;
}
```

| Type     | Default impl                                                 |
|----------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `int`    | Decimal digits (`42` → `#3432`)                              |
| `bytes`  | Hex digits, lower-case, no `0x` prefix (`#deadbeef` → `#6465616462656566`) |
| `bool`   | `#74727565` (`"true"`) or `#66616c7365` (`"false"`)          |
| `string` | UTF-8 bytes (its `encodeUtf8()`)                             |

### Calling it

```ts
const n: int = 42;
trace(n.show());           // emits "42" to the trace log
```

### Implementing it on your own type

Useful for adding debug-friendly trace output without writing a hand-rolled formatter every time:

```ts
struct Account {
    name: bytes,
    balance: int,
}

type Account implements Show {
    show( self ): bytes {
        return self.name.concat( ": " )
            .concat(self.balance.show());
    }
}

const a = Account{ name: "alice", balance: 100 };
trace(a.show());   // "alice: 100"
```

### Using it as a constraint

If you write a generic helper that traces its argument:

```ts
function debugIdentity<T: Show>( x: T ): T {
    trace(x.show());
    return x;
}
```

## Implementation note

Both interfaces are registered in the prelude via the same `populateBuiltinInterfaces` entry point. At call time, dispatch goes through `resolveInterfaceImpl(concreteType, interfaceName)` which:

1. **First** checks the type's `methodsNamesPtr` / `methodNamesPtr` for a user-supplied impl.
2. **Then** falls back to the built-in factory map (`program.builtinInterfaceImpls`).
3. **Otherwise** raises a `"type X does not implement Y"` compile error.

This means **user impls always win** over the built-in derivation. If you write a `type int implements ToData` (which would be unusual but legal), your version replaces the default `iData` lowering for every call site that monomorphises against `int`.

## See also

- [`data`](./Prelude/Data.mdx) — the type `ToData` produces
- [`std.builtins`](./Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx) — the underlying data constructors (`constrData`, `iData`, `bData`, …)
- [Datum & Redeemer Flow](./concepts/Datum%20and%20Redeemer%20Flow.md) — when and where `ToData` is invoked at the on-chain ↔ off-chain boundary


=== onchain/Builtin Values and Literals.md ===

---
sidebar_position: 9
sidebar_label: Builtin Values and Literals
---

# Builtin Values and Literals

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

Every literal form Pebble's tokenizer and parser recognise, plus the small set of implicit bindings the compiler injects into method bodies.

## Integer literals

| Form                 | Example         | Notes                                              |
|----------------------|-----------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| Decimal              | `42`, `-7`, `0` | Arbitrary precision — no overflow.                 |
| Underscore separator | `1_000_000`     | Cosmetic; ignored at parse time.                   |
| Hexadecimal          | `0xCAFE`        | Case-insensitive after `0x`.                       |

All resolve to type [`int`](./Prelude/Int.mdx).

```ts
const big: int = 1_000_000;
const hex: int = 0xCAFE;
const neg: int = -7;
```

## Byte-string literals

| Form           | Example        | Notes                                                            |
|----------------|----------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Hex literal    | `#deadbeef`    | Each pair of hex digits is one byte. Case-insensitive after `#`. |
| Empty          | `#""`          | Zero-length byte string.                                         |
| Double-quoted  | `"hello"`      | Its UTF-8 bytes: `#68656c6c6f`. A `bytes` literal, not a `string`. |

All resolve to type [`bytes`](./Prelude/Bytes.mdx).

```ts
const policy: PolicyId = #cafedead;
const empty:  bytes    = #"";
const utf8:   bytes    = "hello";        // #68656c6c6f
```

## String literals

A quoted literal is **`bytes`**, not `string`. A `string` value comes from
[`std.builtins.decodeUtf8`](./Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx), and `trace` and `fail` accept
either.

```ts
const msg: string = std.builtins.decodeUtf8( "Order filled" );
trace(msg);
```

Escapes (`\n`, `\t`, `\"`, `\\`, etc.) are recognised inside double quotes. There are **no** template strings — concatenate with `+`.

Strings exist primarily for `trace` messages and `fail` reasons — avoid storing large strings
on-chain (every byte costs CPU and memory in the script budget).

## Boolean literals

`true`, `false` — type [`bool`](./Prelude/Boolean.mdx).

```ts
const ok: bool = true;
if( ok ) { trace("ok"); }
```

## Void

`void` is the type of a value that carries nothing: a function that only asserts or traces, and
the statement-like expressions `trace(...)` and `assert ...`. There is **no literal** for it —
`()` is not a value — so a `void` value is the call itself:

```ts
function check( amount: int ): void {
    assert amount > 0 else "amount";
}

const nothing: void = check( 1 );
```

## Array (list) literals

Square-bracketed comma-separated elements:

```ts
const empty: List<int> = [];
const xs:    List<int> = [1, 2, 3];
const nested: List<List<int>> = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];
```

The element type is inferred from the declared type, or from the first element if it's unambiguous. An empty literal `[]` requires an explicit type annotation.

These produce values of type [`List<T>`](./Prelude/List.mdx). To get an [`Array<T>`](./Prelude/Array.mdx) (the random-access form), pass a list through [`std.array.fromList`](./Standard%20Library/std.array.mdx).

## Map literals

Brace-enclosed `key: value` pairs:

```ts
const empty: LinearMap<bytes, int> = {};
const m:     LinearMap<bytes, int> = { #01: 10, #02: 20 };
```

Produces a [`LinearMap<K, V>`](./Prelude/LinearMap.mdx). Order of entries is preserved; duplicates are allowed (matching the underlying assoc-list semantics). A key is any expression except a **bare identifier**: `{ a: 1 }` is a struct's field, so a variable used as a key is written `{ (a): 1 }` (error 30212 otherwise). Without an expected type, the first entry gives the map's type.

## Struct / variant constructors

Construction uses the constructor's name, bare or qualified — for a single-constructor struct the constructor has the struct's own name:

```ts
struct Order {
    owner: PubKeyHash,
    policy: PolicyId,
    amount: int,
}

const o: Order = Order.Order{
    owner: #cafedead,
    policy: #beef1234,
    amount: 100,
};
```

For multi-constructor structs, name the variant:

```ts
struct Shape {
    Circle { r: int }
    Rect { w: int, h: int }
}

const s: Shape = Shape.Circle{ r: 2 };
```

The bare form resolves too when the constructor name is unambiguous (`Circle{ r: 2 }`,
`Order{ owner: …, … }`). `Some{ value: 1 }` and `None{}` are expressions, like any other
constructor: `Optional` has no qualifier (`Optional.Some{ … }` does not resolve).

## Implicit bindings inside method bodies

The compiler injects two implicit names into the body of any `contract` method (`spend`, `mint`, `certify`, `withdraw`, `propose`, `vote`):

### `context: ScriptContext`

The full script context for the current invocation. Destructure it for the fields you actually need:

```ts
contract Vault {
    spend handler( amount: int ) {
        const { tx, spendingRef, optionalDatum } = context;
        // tx            — the full Tx
        // spendingRef   — the TxOutRef of the input being spent
        // optionalDatum — the raw datum of that input
        assert amount > 0;
    }
}
```

The redeemer is **not** in `context`: a method's parameters are its redeemer fields. `purpose` is
not available either (error 294): the purpose is the method you are in.

For `spend` methods, additional fields are available:

| Field              | Type                  | Notes                                                    |
|--------------------|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `tx`               | `Tx`                  | The full transaction.                                    |
| `spendingRef`      | `TxOutRef`            | The reference of the UTxO being spent.                   |
| `optionalDatum`    | `Optional<data>`      | The raw datum, when no `state` is in scope.              |
| `state`            | `<sum of states>`     | Present only inside a `spend` method declared on a [`state`](./State.md). |

See [Validators 101](./concepts/Validators%20101.md) for the full per-purpose breakdown.

### `this`

Reserved for future use in method-on-type forms (e.g. user-defined `impl Foo { ... }`). Not generally available today.

## `fail` expression

`fail` is both a statement and an expression. As a statement it aborts the script unconditionally with an optional trace message:

```ts
fail;                                 // bare abort
fail "missing datum";                 // abort with a string message in the trace
fail "expected: " + expected.show();  // abort with a dynamic message
```

The expression form (i.e. `fail` appearing in expression position) has type `void` — it never produces a value because it never returns.

## `undefined`

`undefined` is a reserved identifier that produces a value of any type. It's used only by the compiler in synthesised IR; user code should not reference it. Reading from it at runtime aborts the script.

## See also

- [Prelude Types](/category/prelude-types) — what each literal form produces
- [Syntax / Control Flow Statements](./Syntax/Control%20Flow%20Statements.md) — `if`, `for`, `while`, `match`, `return`, `assert`, `trace`, `fail`
- [Contract Statements](./Contract%20Statements.md) — where `context` and per-purpose extras come from


=== onchain/CLI.md ===

---
sidebar_position: 15
---

# CLI

The `pebble` command-line tool is the official utility for working with Pebble projects. It
compiles a project, exports a single function, runs tests, debugs one evaluation and starts a
REPL, in the project of the working directory.

```bash
# if installed globally
npm install -g @harmoniclabs/pebble-cli

# then
pebble <command>

# or, use `npx` / direct node invocation if you prefer not to install globally
npx pebble <command>
```

This page documents `@harmoniclabs/pebble-cli` 0.6.0.

## Commands

| Command               | What it does                                                      |
|-----------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`help`](#help)       | display help for `pebble` commands                                |
| [`version`](#version) | the CLI and language versions, and the commit hash                 |
| [`init`](#init)       | create a fresh Pebble project                                      |
| [`compile`](#compile) | compile the project: `out.flat` and `out.flat.map`                 |
| [`export`](#export)   | compile and export a single function                               |
| [`test`](#test)       | discover and run `test name() { ... }` blocks                      |
| [`repl`](#repl)       | an interactive session in the project of the working directory     |
| [`debug`](#debug)     | one evaluation, statement by statement                             |
| [`uplc`](#uplc)       | utilities for flat-encoded UPLC files                              |

`pebble --version` is `pebble version`. `pebble <command> --help` prints the flags of one command.

## `help`

```bash
pebble help
```

## `version`

Outputs the CLI version, the language version and the commit hash of the build.

```bash
pebble version
pebble --version
```

```text
pebble-cli version:      0.6.0
pebble language version: 0.6.0
commit hash:             4374aea5e466396ce524dcf7dffa348adf7c75f9
```

## `init`

Creates a new directory with a fresh Pebble project, including a `pebble.config.json`.

```bash
pebble init
```

## `compile`

Compiles the project's entry file into `out.flat` and writes its
[source map](./Debugging.md#source-maps) next to it.

```bash
pebble compile [options]
```

| Option           | Default                | Meaning                                                            |
|------------------|------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `-c, --config`   | `./pebble.config.json` | the config file                                                     |
| `--entry <file>` | `./index.pebble`       | the entry `.pebble` file — used **only if missing** from the config  |
| `-o, --output`   | `./out.flat`           | the output file — used **only if missing** from the config           |

```bash
pebble compile --config ./pebble.config.json

# or with explicit entry and output
pebble compile --entry ./src/contracts/MyContract.pebble -o ./build/MyContract.flat
```

With `-o build/MyContract.flat` the map is written as `build/MyContract.flat.map`.

The entry file must declare a `contract`: `compile` produces that contract's script. To compile a
single function instead, use [`export`](#export).

Output:

```text
compiled program written to ./out/out.flat
source map written to ./out/out.flat.map
```

Warnings are printed and the script is written; errors print `compilation failed: N errors`
(`1 error` when there is one) and the command exits `1`. See [Diagnostics](./reference/Diagnostics.md).

See [Compiler Configuration](./Compiler%20Configuration.md) for the full `pebble.config.json`
schema.

## `export`

Compiles the project and writes **one function** as a standalone script — the form you apply
parameters to and deploy, or a helper you evaluate off-chain.

```bash
pebble export --function-name myValidator
```

| Option                   | Meaning                                                          |
|--------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--function-name <name>` | the function to export (required)                                  |
| `-c, --config`           | the config file (default `./pebble.config.json`)                   |
| `--entry <file>`         | the entry `.pebble` file — **overwrites** the config's value        |
| `-o, --output`           | the output file — **overwrites** the config's value                 |

An exported function is compiled without the script marker (`addMarker`), and gets its map the
same way `compile` does.

## `test`

Discovers `test name() { ... }` blocks under `[path]` (default: the current directory) and runs
them, reporting the cost of each.

```bash
pebble test [options] [path]
```

| Option                          | Default                | Meaning                                                        |
|---------------------------------|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `-c, --config`                  | `./pebble.config.json` | the config file                                                  |
| `--testPathPattern <regex>`     | —                      | run only files whose path matches the regex                      |
| `-t, --testNamePattern <regex>` | —                      | run only tests whose name matches the regex                      |
| `--property-runs <n>`           | `100`                  | iterations per property test                                     |
| `--seed <int>`                  | `0`                    | seed for the property-test PRNG                                  |
| `--json`                        | off                    | machine-readable results on stdout instead of the human report   |
| `--bail`                        | off                    | stop after the first failing test file                           |

```bash
pebble test --testNamePattern "add" --property-runs 1000 --seed 42
```

A failing test prints the location of the failure and the open calls; see [Testing](./Testing.md)
for the output and for how to write tests.

## `repl`

Starts an interactive session in the project of the working directory. Each line runs as one
program: the declarations entered so far, then the line.

```bash
pebble repl [options]
```

| Option         | Default                                                        | Meaning         |
|----------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------|
| `-c, --config` | the nearest `pebble.config.json`, from the working directory up | the config file |

The project's options come from that config, and imports resolve from the working directory. The
REPL writes nothing: no `out.flat`, no map.

```text
pebble> import { entry } from "./src/index.pebble";
pebble> entry( 20 )
40
cpu: 472343 | mem: 2203
```

### What a line can be

| Line                  | Behaviour                                                                                            |
|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| expression            | prints the value and its cost — `1 + 2`, `factorial( 5 )`                                               |
| declaration           | `const`, `let`, `function`, `struct`, `import`, `contract`: kept for the lines after                    |
| statement             | `if`, `for`, `while`, `trace`, `assert`, `fail`, `x = ...`: run, and what they change in a `let` is kept |
| `test name() { ... }` | runs at once, reports PASS or FAIL with the location, and is **not** kept                                |
| `contract C { ... }`  | type-checked; its methods need a script context, so they run under `pebble test`                         |

- Redeclaring a name replaces it: a `let` is shadowed, so its type may change.
- Functions and contracts can use the session's constants and other declarations — not its `let`s.
- A statement that changes a `let` (`total += x`, a loop) is kept, so later lines see the change.
- A line that fails changes nothing.
- Declarations print nothing, but are computed on their line, so `const z = 1 / 0;` fails there.

Values print with their Pebble type:

```text
pebble> const m: LinearMap<bytes, int> = { #01: 10, #02: 20 };
pebble> m
{ #01: 10, #02: 20 }
cpu: 988880 | mem: 5156
```

### Errors and tests

Every diagnostic of the line is reported, with the line underlined. A failing `assert` or builtin
shows where it failed — also inside a function entered earlier, or in an imported file — and the
open calls:

```text
pebble> test my_test() { assert 1 == 2; }
FAIL my_test  [cpu: 80100, mem: 600]
  error: explicit error from uplc
  1 | test my_test() { assert 1 == 2; }
    |                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

### Commands

| Command  | Meaning                                                   |
|----------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| `:help`  | the help text                                             |
| `:list`  | the declarations kept                                     |
| `:reset` | forget every declaration                                  |
| `:quit`  | exit (also `Ctrl+D`, or `Ctrl+C` twice on an empty line)  |

`Ctrl+C` drops the line being typed. History is kept in `~/.pebble_repl_history`;
`PEBBLE_REPL_HISTORY` moves it, and an empty value turns it off.

A line can spend the mainnet per-transaction limit — 10,000,000,000 cpu and 16,500,000 mem — so
an endless loop stops with `out of budget` instead of hanging the session.

### Piped input

Lines can be piped in: they run in order, the output reads as a session, and the exit code is `1`
if any line failed.

```bash
printf 'const n = 3;\nn * n\n' | pebble repl
```

`ReplSession` is the same REPL without a terminal, for other tools: `eval( line )` returns the
value, the diagnostics and the failure with positions in the line, the logs, the budget and the
tests' results.

## `debug`

Records **one** evaluation and prints it statement by statement, in source order, with the values
of the variables: a test (`--test`) or a script evaluation buildooor saved (`--eval`).

```bash
pebble debug --test small_input
```

```text
test small_input  src/index.test.pebble: 3 steps, failed at step 3

test small_input  src/index.test.pebble
  #1    4  const r = entry( 5 )                              r = <not evaluated>
           → entry  src/index.pebble
  #2    7    const v = check( x )                            v = <not evaluated>
             → check  src/index.pebble
  #3    2      assert x > 10 else "x must be greater than 10";  <- failed
                 x = 5
failed: explicit error from uplc (cpu 413390, mem 2401)
trace: x must be greater than 10
```

| Option                | Default                | Meaning                                                                    |
|-----------------------|------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `-c, --config`        | `./pebble.config.json` | the config file                                                              |
| `--test <name>`       | —                      | debug the test with this name, or part of it, among the tests of `[path]`     |
| `--eval <file>`       | —                      | replay a saved script evaluation (buildooor's `saveFailedEvaluations`)        |
| `--step <n>`          | —                      | print step `n` in full: the open calls and every variable with its whole value |
| `--all`               | off                    | list the variables in scope at every step                                     |
| `--json`              | off                    | emit the steps, the variables and the result as JSON                          |
| `--max-states <n>`    | `2000000`              | record at most `n` machine states                                             |
| `--property-runs <n>` | `100`                  | iterations of a property test to look for a failure in                        |
| `--seed <int>`        | `0`                    | seed for the property-test PRNG                                               |

It exits `0` whenever the evaluation could be shown, passed or failed.

See [Debugging](./Debugging.md) for what the steps are, for the source maps behind them and for
replaying a failed transaction's evaluation.

## `uplc`

Utilities for UPLC programs stored in flat-encoded files.

```bash
pebble uplc pretty [options]
```

| Option         | Default          | Meaning                                                                                                  |
|----------------|------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `-i, --input`  | `./out/out.flat` | the input flat-encoded UPLC file                                                                            |
| `-o, --output` | —                | the output file (extension `.uplc`); prints to the console when missing                                     |
| `--canonical`  | off              | emit spec-compliant UPLC concrete syntax (parseable by `plutus-core`) instead of Pebble's richer format      |

```bash
pebble uplc pretty -i out/out.flat -o out/out.uplc
```

## See also

- [Compiler Configuration](./Compiler%20Configuration.md) — the `pebble.config.json` schema
- [Testing](./Testing.md) — writing tests, the runner's output, fuzzers and shrinking
- [Debugging](./Debugging.md) — source maps, traces, `pebble debug`
- [Installation](../Installation.md) — installing the CLI and the editor extension


=== onchain/Compiler Configuration.md ===

---
sidebar_position: 16
---

# Compiler Configuration

The Pebble compiler reads its options from a `pebble.config.json` file at the root of your project. The [CLI](./CLI.md) resolves it relative to the current working directory and defaults to `./pebble.config.json`. You can point to a different file with the `--config` flag.

## Example

```json
{
  "compilerVersion": "^0.6.0",
  "entry": "./src/index.pebble",
  "outDir": "./out",
  "removeTraces": true,
  "sourceMap": true
}
```

`pebble init` generates a working `pebble.config.json` for you.

## Fields

### `compilerVersion`

**Required since `0.2.0`.** Type: `string` (npm-style semver range).

The compiler validates this range against its own version at startup and throws if it does not satisfy it. A missing or empty value is treated as invalid.

```json
{ "compilerVersion": "^0.6.0" }
```

See [Supported semver syntax](#supported-semver-syntax) below for the accepted range forms.

:::caution Migration from 0.1.x → 0.2.0
Projects created on Pebble `0.1.x` did not include `compilerVersion`. Add it to your `pebble.config.json` before upgrading the compiler, otherwise you will see:

```
Error: Pebble compiler config is missing "compilerVersion". Starting from
@harmoniclabs/pebble@0.2.0 this field is required and must be an npm-style
semver range (e.g. "^0.2.0").
```

If your compiler version does not satisfy the configured range:

```
Error: Pebble compiler version 0.2.0 does not satisfy the configured
"compilerVersion" range "^0.3.0".
```
:::

### `entry`

Type: `string`. Default: `"./src/index.pebble"`.

Path to the entry `.pebble` file, relative to `root`.

### `root`

Type: `string`. Default: `"."`.

Path to the project root. All other relative paths in the config are resolved against this.

### `outDir`

Type: `string`. Default: `"./out"`.

Directory where the compiler writes its output (the compiled `out.flat` and related artefacts).

### `silent`

Type: `boolean`. Default: `false`.

When `true`, suppresses compiler stdout output. Useful for embedding the compiler programmatically.

### `targetUplcVersion`

Type: `UPLCVersion`. Default: the current default UPLC version exported by `@harmoniclabs/uplc`.

The UPLC version that gets encoded into the compiled script. Most users should leave this at the default.

### `removeTraces`

Type: `boolean`. Default: `true` (the production options).

When `true`, the compiled script has no `trace` statements and no messages of `assert` and
`fail`: it is smaller and cheaper, and has a new hash. The failures stay — an `assert` that fails
still fails, with the error of a script that had no message.

The traces are removed **before** anything is optimized, so the program is byte for byte the one
the source without them compiles to: a value computed only for a trace is not computed, and the
optimizer is free to drop a branch that only failed with a message.

The [source map](./Debugging.md#traces-are-removed-from-the-script-and-kept-in-the-map) keeps
them, so `pebble test`, `pebble debug`, buildooor and `evaluateWithSourceMap` still print them
where they would have run, in order with the traces the program kept. A message computed from
values is computed on the side, from the values the program holds at that point.

Set it to `false` to keep the traces inside the script — useful when the script is inspected by a
node or a tool that does not read source maps.

:::caution output change in 0.6.0
Before 0.6.0 the option was never read, so every build kept its traces. A contract compiled with
the default now gets smaller (UPLC-CAPE's `two_party_escrow`: 1354 → 853 bytes) and a **new
hash** — recompile and compare hashes before relying on a script address.
:::

### `sourceMap`

Type: `boolean`. Default: `true`.

Writes a source map next to the compiled script: `out/out.flat.map` next to `out/out.flat`, and
`<output>.map` with `-o`. The map never changes the script: maps on or off, the bytes are
identical.

`pebble test`, `pebble debug` and buildooor read it to report a failure at
its line and column in the source. See [Debugging](./Debugging.md#source-maps).

### `sourceMapContent`

Type: `boolean`. Default: `false`.

Includes the sources' texts in the map (`sourcesContent`), so a tool can print the failing line
without access to the sources.

### `delayHoists`

Type: `boolean`. Default: `true`.

When `true`, hoisted closed terms are converted to `letted` terms instead of being unconditionally added to the script's roots.

Hoisted terms are blindly included as part of the script's initialization, so unused hoists in some branches (common in multi-purpose scripts) still pay the initialization cost. Lettings move that cost into the branches that actually use the term, at the price of slightly higher compilation time.

Recommended `true` for production builds.

### `uplcOptimizations`

Type: `object`. A bag of fine-grained UPLC optimization flags. Default fields:

- `groupApplications: boolean` (default `true`) — group sequential applications into single applications where possible.
- `inlineSingleUse: boolean` (default `true`) — inline terms that are used exactly once.
- `simplifyWrappedPartialFuncApps: boolean` (default `true`) — simplify partial function applications wrapped inside other terms.
- `removeForceDelay: boolean` (default `true`) — collapse `force (delay x)` pairs.

You can override individual flags:

```json
{
  "uplcOptimizations": {
    "inlineSingleUse": false
  }
}
```

The other flags fall back to their defaults.

### `addMarker`

Type: `boolean`. Default: `true`.

When `true`, the compiler emits a script marker (used by tooling to identify Pebble-generated scripts). Disable for size-sensitive deployments where the marker is not needed.

### `encodingStrategy`

`"minimal" | "legacy"` — default `"minimal"` *(since 0.5.0)*.

Picks the data encoding of single-constructor structs declared in the
**shortcut** form (`struct S { a: int }`):

- `"minimal"` — a list of fields, `List [ … ]`.
- `"legacy"` — `Constr 0 [ … ]`, as every compiler up to 0.4.x did. Set
  this to recompile an already-deployed contract to the same bytes.

The option only decides the default. In the source, the explicit form
(`struct S { S { a: int } }`) is always `Constr 0 [ … ]` and the
`untagged` keyword always gives the list; see
[Types](./Types.md#on-chain-encoding). `"default"`, the pre-0.5.0
spelling of `"legacy"`, is still accepted.

```json
{
  "compilerVersion": "^0.6.0",
  "encodingStrategy": "legacy"
}
```

### `targetPlutusVersion`

*Since 0.5.0.* `"v3" | "experimental-v4"` — default `"v3"`. Case-insensitive.

The context type names never change — `ScriptContext`, `Tx`, `TxIn`,
`TxOut`, `Address`, `ScriptInfo`, `ScriptPurpose` — this option decides
which Plutus ledger-API family **defines** them (exactly one family
exists per compilation; there are no suffixed variants and no mixing):

- `"v3"` — the stable Conway-era types: what runs on-chain today
  (protocol version 11 executes PlutusV3 scripts).
- `"experimental-v4"` — the Dijkstra-era types, mirroring
  plutus-ledger-api 1.71.0.0 (nested-transaction guards, accounts, the
  4-field script context, and product types encoded as a list of fields
  instead of `Constr 0`). The Dijkstra hard fork has not happened yet
  and CIP-0118 is still Proposed, so these shapes may track upstream
  changes — the `experimental-` prefix is deliberate. The plain `"v4"`
  spelling is reserved until Plutus V4 is active on mainnet and is
  rejected with guidance; once the fork lands it becomes the name (and
  `"experimental-v4"` will keep working as an alias).

Flipping the target re-types the same source against the other context
shape — code that only touches fields both families share keeps
compiling, and anything version-specific surfaces as a normal type
error.

```json
{
  "compilerVersion": "^0.6.0",
  "targetPlutusVersion": "experimental-v4"
}
```

:::caution
No public network runs Plutus V4 scripts yet, so nothing compiled with
`"experimental-v4"` can be deployed. The shapes have already changed
twice between upstream releases (1.68 to 1.69, then 1.71) and may change again
before the hard fork.
:::

## Programmatic options

The package exports the option templates it uses, so a tool embedding the compiler does not have
to spell every field:

| Export               | Contents                                                                 |
|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `productionOptions`  | `removeTraces: true`, `delayHoists: true`, production optimizations, marker on |
| `defaultOptions`     | the same as `productionOptions`; the base of `completeCompilerOptions`     |
| `testOptions`        | `productionOptions` with `silent: true` — what `pebble test` uses          |
| `debugOptions`       | `removeTraces: false`, `delayHoists: false`, no inlining, marker off        |

The CLI bases its own configuration on `productionOptions`.

`completeCompilerOptions( partial )` fills the missing fields from `defaultOptions`. Note that
none of the templates carries `compilerVersion`: every caller sets it, so a missing or
unsatisfied range always surfaces as an error from the `Compiler` constructor.

## Supported semver syntax

`compilerVersion` accepts a subset of the npm semver range grammar, sufficient for pinning the compiler in real projects:

| Form | Example | Matches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exact | `0.2.0` | only `0.2.0` |
| Comparator | `>=0.2.0`, `>0.2.0`, `<=0.3.0`, `<0.3.0`, `=0.2.0` | versions satisfying the comparator |
| Caret | `^0.2.0` | `>=0.2.0 <0.3.0` (pre-1.0 caret pins the minor; `^1.2.3` → `>=1.2.3 <2.0.0`) |
| Tilde | `~0.2.0` | `>=0.2.0 <0.3.0` |
| Wildcards | `*`, `x`, `0.x`, `0.2.x` | any matching the wildcard pattern |
| Hyphen range | `0.2.0 - 0.3.0` | `>=0.2.0 <=0.3.0` |
| AND | `>=0.2.0 <0.4.0` | all comparators must hold (separated by whitespace) |
| OR | `^0.2.0 \|\| ^0.3.0` | any sub-range must hold (separated by `\|\|`) |

:::info
Prerelease and build-metadata suffixes (`0.2.0-beta`, `0.2.0+build.1`) are accepted but ignored — only the numeric `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` core is compared. The Pebble compiler ships plain `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` releases.
:::


=== onchain/Contract Statements.md ===

---
sidebar_position: 4
sidebar_label: Contract Statements
---

# Contract

A **contract** in Pebble is the top-level unit of on-chain logic.  

It defines one or more **validators** (entry points), which are compiled into Plutus Core scripts.
 
Contracts are declared using the `contract` keyword. Inside a contract you declare **validators** — functions that define the on-chain logic.

Syntax:
<!-- no-compile: syntax skeleton -->
```ts
contract ContractName {
    // one or more validator statements
    spend validatorName(...) { ... }
    mint validatorName(...) { ... }
    ...
}
```

- `ContractName` must be unique within a compilation unit.
- Each validator compiles into a separate script that can be deployed on-chain.



## Context

Inside a contract, Pebble automatically provides a context binding called `context`. This represents the current script execution context and gives access to transaction information.


:::info
`context` is not a normal variable, it is a special keyword. It’s a synthetic binding automatically injected by the compiler to let you access the current validator execution environment.

The compiler internally uses a construct called contextVarsMapping to resolve the fields that can be extracted from context.

You cannot reassign or shadow it — it’s purely a read-only view into the validator’s execution context.
:::

The shape of context depends on the validator purpose.


Inside each validator, a context object provides:

- `tx` : Transaction
- purpose-specific fields (`spendingRef` for `spend`, `policy` for `mint`, etc. — see below)
- for `spend` validators: `optionalDatum` (and `state` inside [`state`](./State.md) blocks)

Each validator function inside a contract is independent — compilation produces one Plutus script per validator.

Context is immutable — you can destructure it, but not reassign.

The available fields in context vary depending on the validator purpose. Pebble enforces correct context usage at compile time.

#### Example:
```ts
contract OnlySpend {
    spend allowSpending() {
        const { tx, spendingRef } = context;

        // simple always-valid contract
        assert true;
    }
}
```
Here, the contract is `OnlySpend`. It has a single `spend` validator `allowSpending`. `context` is a keyword bound to the spending validator context. 

In the contract body, the `context` is destructured to access the transaction (`tx`) and the reference of the input being spent (`spendingRef`).



## Contract Parameters

Pebble contracts can take **parameters** at declaration time.  
These are values that are **fixed at contract instantiation** and become part of the compiled script hash.

This is useful when you want to bind a contract to a specific constant, like an owner’s public key or a fixed configuration (e.g., fee rate)

<!-- no-compile: syntax skeleton -->
```ts
contract ContractName {
    param param1: Type;
    param param2: Type;
    // ...

    // validator definitions
}
```

Each parameter is declared on its own line inside the contract body using the `param` keyword, followed by a name, a `:` type, and a terminating `;`. Parameters must appear before the validator (`spend` / `mint` / etc.) declarations. They are available inside every validator of the contract.

Parameters are immutable once compiled, i.e. they cannot be changed without recompiling the contract.

Hence, it is ideal to use parameters for constants known at deployment time, and not for values that change per transaction.

Contract parameters are especially useful for  Single-owner scripts (binding a contract to a fixed PubKeyHash), Policy scripts (tying to a fixed minting policy).

### Applying parameters off-chain (the parameter ABI)

The compiled script is a function of its parameters: apply them as UPLC
constants (in declaration order, before the script context) to obtain the
deployable script.

Each parameter must be applied as its **runtime representation**:

| param type | apply as |
|---|---|
| `int` | a UPLC **integer** constant |
| `bytes` | a UPLC **bytestring** constant |
| `boolean` | a UPLC **bool** constant |
| data-encoded types (`Address`, `TxOutRef`, structs, `data`, ...) | a UPLC **data** constant |

:::caution scalars are NOT wrapped in Data
Most Cardano tooling (`applyParamsToScript` in Lucid, MeshJS, Aiken's
`apply`, ...) wraps **every** parameter as Plutus Data. Pebble scalars are
native constants instead: wrapping a `bytes` param in `DataB` (or an `int`
in `DataI`) produces a script that **fails at a distance** during phase-2
validation — e.g. `lengthOfByteString :: not BS` the first time the
parameter is used — because the validator reads the parameter as its
native type without decoding.

```ts
// off-chain (buildooor / @harmoniclabs/uplc), for
// `param owner: bytes; param genesisUtxo: TxOutRef;`
body = new Application( body, UPLCConst.byteString( ownerHash ) );    // bytes -> native
body = new Application( body, UPLCConst.data( txOutRefData( ref ) ) ); // struct -> data
```
:::



## Validators 

Functions that define the on-chain logic.

Supported validator types:

- `spend` – Spending validator
- `mint` – Minting policy
- `certify` – Certificate validator
- `withdraw` – Withdrawal validator
- `propose` – Governance proposal validator
- `vote` – Governance vote validator
- `guard` – Guard validator (Plutus V4 / Dijkstra guarding purpose, CIP-0112 & CIP-0118); requires `targetPlutusVersion: "experimental-v4"` — see [Compiler Configuration](./Compiler%20Configuration.md#targetplutusversion)




## Context for each Validator

The shape of `context depends on the validator purpose:

The **redeemer** never appears in `context`: a validator's redeemer fields are its
**method parameters**.

### For `spend` validators
```ts
{
    tx: Tx,
    spendingRef: TxOutRef,          // reference of the input being spent
    optionalDatum: Optional<data>,
    state: /* the matched state */  // only inside `state` blocks
}
```

### For `mint` validators:
```ts
{
    tx: Tx,
    policy: bytes   // this script's minting policy hash
}
```

### For `certify` validators:
```ts
{
    tx: Tx,
    certificateIndex: int,
    certificate: Certificate
}
```

### For `withdraw` validators:
```ts
{
    tx: Tx,
    policy: bytes   // the withdrawing (script) credential hash
}
```

### For `propose` validators:
```ts
{
    tx: Tx,
    proposalIndex: int,
    proposal: ProposalProcedure
}
```

### For `vote` validators:
```ts
{
    tx: Tx,
    voter: Voter
}
```

### For `guard` validators (Plutus V4 only):
```ts
{
    tx: Tx,
    guardIndex: int,
    topTxInfo: Optional<TopTxInfo>
}
```

`topTxInfo` is how a guard learns *where* it runs: `Some{ value: top }` means
the top level of a nested-transaction batch (`top.subTransactions` and the
aggregated `top.simplified` describe the whole batch), `None{}` means the
guard is executing inside a sub-transaction. `guard` methods are rejected
under the default `"v3"` target with a diagnostic naming the option, and
are not allowed inside `state` blocks.

<!-- target: experimental-v4 -->
```ts
contract Batch {
    guard check() {
        const { guardIndex, topTxInfo } = context;
        match topTxInfo {
            when Some{ value: top }: {
                assert std.list.length( top.subTransactions ) <= 4 else "batch too large";
            }
            when None{}: { /* sub-transaction guard */ }
        }
    }
}
```


## Execution levels: `top` / `nested` (Plutus V4)

With nested transactions (CIP-0118) a script may run in the **top-level**
transaction of a batch or **inside a sub-transaction**. Every contract
method declares the level it is valid at by prefixing the purpose keyword:

<!-- no-compile -->
```ts
contract Escrow {
    top spend settle() { ... }        // valid only in the top-level transaction
    nested spend deposit() { ... }    // valid only inside a sub-transaction
    mint issue() { ... }              // no level keyword = `top`
    nested guard check() { ... }
}
```

The compiled validator matches the transaction's `tx.subTxIx` **before**
the purpose: `None` dispatches the `top` methods, `Some{ value }` the
`nested` ones, and a level with no methods fails unconditionally. So **a
contract written without any level keyword is top-only and always fails
when executed inside a sub-transaction** — that is the safe default.
Levels apply to `state` spend methods as well, and they never change the
redeemer encoding (a contract compiled with explicit `top` keywords is
byte-identical to one without).

Requires `targetPlutusVersion: "experimental-v4"` for `nested`; under the
default `"v3"` target `nested` is rejected with a diagnostic naming the
option, while `top` is accepted as a no-op. Both words remain usable as
ordinary identifiers.

## Method names

All validators declared **directly** in the contract body share one redeemer union (one constructor per method), so their names must be **unique across all purposes** — `spend foo` and `mint foo` in the same contract is a compile error. Methods inside a [`state`](./State.md) block only need unique names within their own state.

## Exporting a contract

Since `0.3.7` a contract can be exported:

```ts
export contract Vault { ... }
```

This exports the contract's **type-level symbols** — its state-datum union (`Vault`, `Vault.SomeState`) and its redeemer unions (`redeemerof Vault`, `redeemerof Vault.SomeState`) — so *other* contracts can decode its datums and redeemers. No code is exported, and the validator bodies of an imported contract are never compiled.

See [Cross-Contract Types](./Cross-Contract%20Types.md) for the full picture.


=== onchain/Cross-Contract Types.md ===

---
sidebar_position: 6
sidebar_label: Cross-Contract Types
---

# Cross-contract types — `export contract` and `redeemerof`

*Available since compiler `0.3.7`.*

A validator often needs to inspect **another contract's** UTxOs or redeemers: checking that an output sits at a partner script with a well-formed datum, or that a reference input's state matches an expectation. To do that safely you need the other contract's **data shapes** — its datum and redeemer types — without copy-pasting mirror structs by hand.

Pebble exposes them through two pieces:

- `export contract` makes a contract's **type-level symbols** importable;
- the `redeemerof` type operator names its **redeemer unions**.

## Exporting a contract

```ts
// vault.pebble
export contract Vault {
    state Locked {
        owner: bytes
        amount: int

        spend withdraw( part: int ) { /* ... */ }
        spend close() { /* ... */ }
    }
    state Idle {
        owner: bytes
    }

    mint open( amount: int ) { /* ... */ }
    mint burn() { /* ... */ }
}
```

`export contract` does **not** export any code. It exports the contract's *types*, derived from its **method signatures only**:

| symbol | what it is |
|---|---|
| `Vault` | the **state-datum union**: one constructor per `state`, fields = the state's fields |
| `Vault.Locked` | the union **narrowed** to one state (decoding checks that state's constructor tag) |
| `redeemerof Vault` | the union of the contract's **direct methods** (see below) |
| `redeemerof Vault.Locked` | the union of that **state's `spend` methods** |

Because only signatures are read, importing a contract never compiles its validator bodies — cross-contract type access adds nothing to your script and nothing of yours to theirs.

A contract **without** `export` stays completely opaque: it cannot be imported, and none of the symbols above exist for it.

:::info stateless contracts
A contract with no `state` blocks has no datum type: using its name in type position is a compile error (`30206`). Its `redeemerof` union still works.
:::

## Importing and using the datum types

```ts
// main.pebble
import { Vault } from "./vault.pebble";

contract Main {
    spend s( redeemer: data ) {
        const { tx } = context;
        const InlineDatum{ datum: od } = tx.outputs[0].datum;

        // whole union: match over the states
        match ( od as Vault ) {
            when Locked{ owner, amount }: { assert amount > 0; }
            when Idle{ owner }: { assert owner.length() == 28; }
        }

        // or decode ONE state directly — the constructor tag is checked,
        // decoding a different state fails at runtime
        const Locked{ owner, amount } = od as Vault.Locked;
    }
}
```

`import * as lib from "./vault.pebble";` works too: `lib.Vault`, `lib.Vault.Locked`, `redeemerof lib.Vault`.

## `redeemerof`

```ts
import { Vault } from "./vault.pebble";

// the direct-methods union: one constructor per method,
// fields = the method's parameters
match ( rdmr as redeemerof Vault ) {
    when open{ amount }: { /* ... */ }
    when burn{}: { /* ... */ }
}

// a state's spend-methods union
```
