```ts
match ( rdmr as redeemerof Vault.Locked ) {
    when withdraw{ part }: { /* ... */ }
    when close{}: { /* ... */ }
}
```

`redeemerof` applies to a **contract** or a **contract state** — never to a single method. A method is one *constructor* of the union, so "the redeemer of `withdraw`" is spelled by matching (or destructuring) that constructor:

```ts
const withdraw{ part } = rdmr as redeemerof Vault.Locked;
```

`redeemerof C.method` is a dedicated compile error (`30205`).

:::info contextual keyword
`redeemerof` is only special in type position when followed by a name — a user type actually called `redeemerof` keeps working.
:::

### Naming the result

`redeemerof` produces an ordinary (data-encoded) struct type; name it with a **`type` alias**:

```ts
type VaultRedeemer  = redeemerof Vault;
type LockedRedeemer = redeemerof Vault.Locked;

// behaves like any struct type from here on:
struct Wrapped { W { inner: VaultRedeemer } }

const open{ amount } = d as VaultRedeemer.open;   // constructor narrowing
```

`using X = ...` is a **namespace** alias and cannot name a type — use `type`.

## Method names and redeemer encoding

All of a contract's **direct** methods (declared straight in the contract body, any purpose) share **one** redeemer union. Two consequences:

1. **Direct method names must be unique across all purposes** — `spend foo` and `mint foo` in one contract is a compile error (`30200`). State `spend` methods only need uniqueness *within their own state* (each state has its own union), so a state method may share a name with a direct method or with another state's method.

2. The union's constructor tags follow the order **spend, mint, withdraw, certify, propose, vote** (declaration order within each purpose). A contract whose direct methods live under a **single purpose** — the common case — keeps exactly the same on-chain encoding as before `0.3.7`.

:::caution encoding change in 0.3.7
Contracts with direct methods under **multiple purposes** changed their on-chain redeemer encoding in `0.3.7`: previously each purpose had its own union with tags restarting at 0; now the tags are unique across all direct methods. Redeploy such contracts and update their off-chain code. Single-purpose contracts and per-state redeemers are byte-identical.
:::

A **single-method** contract (or single-`spend`-method state) is no exception: its redeemer is `Constr 0 [ args... ]`. Contract redeemers and datums are always constructor-encoded, independently of how user-declared structs are encoded.

## Circular imports

Two contracts that validate *each other's* UTxOs need to import each other — a cycle. This is allowed as long as only **types and contracts** cross the cycle:

```ts
// a.pebble                                // b.pebble
import { B } from "./b.pebble";            import { A } from "./a.pebble";

export contract A {                        export contract B {
    state Holding {                            state Pending {
        owner: bytes                               n: int
        spend release( amount: int ) {             spend accept() {
            /* decodes B.Pending */                    /* decodes A.Holding */
        }                                          }
    }                                          }
}                                          }
```

Under the hood, a file inside a cycle first runs a *types-only* pass (types, `type` aliases, interfaces, exported-contract symbols) so its cycle mates can bind those; its functions and constants compile when its own turn comes. Importing a **function or constant** from a module that is still mid-cycle is a compile error (`6056`: *"circular import may only reference types and contracts"*).

Mutually-recursive **struct field** definitions across a cycle are not supported.

## Diagnostics reference

| code | meaning |
|---|---|
| `30200` | duplicate method name across purposes (or within one state) |
| `30201` | `redeemerof` applied to something that is not an (exported) contract |
| `30202` | contract has no direct methods → no `redeemerof C` |
| `30203` | `redeemerof C.State`: no such state |
| `30204` | `redeemerof C.State`: state has no `spend` methods |
| `30205` | `redeemerof` applied to a method (or deeper path) |
| `30206` | stateless contract used as a datum type |
| `6056` | value (function/const) imported across a circular back edge |

## See also

- [Contract Statements](./Contract%20Statements.md) — the `contract` declaration itself
- [`state`](./State.md) — state blocks and their datum encoding
- [Datum & Redeemer Flow](./concepts/Datum%20and%20Redeemer%20Flow.md) — how datums and redeemers cross the on-chain boundary
- [Top-Level Statements](./Syntax/Top%20Level%20Statements.md) — imports, exports and `type` aliases


=== onchain/Debugging.md ===

---
sidebar_position: 18
---

# Debugging

*Pebble 0.6.0.*

Three tools answer "why did my script fail": the [REPL](./CLI.md#repl) while you write, the
location `pebble test` prints when a test fails, and `pebble debug`, which replays one
evaluation statement by statement.

The three rest on the same two artefacts: the **source map** the compiler writes next to the
script, and the **debug information** the compiler keeps in memory.

## Source maps

`pebble compile` and `pebble export` write a source map next to the script: `out/out.flat.map`
next to `out/out.flat`, and `<output>.map` with `-o`.

```bash
pebble compile
ls out
# out.flat  out.flat.map
```

The map never changes the script: with maps on or off, the compiled bytes are identical.

### Options

| Option             | Default | Meaning                                                                 |
|--------------------|---------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `sourceMap`        | `true`  | Write the map next to the script.                                        |
| `sourceMapContent` | `false` | Include the sources' texts (`sourcesContent`), so a tool can print the failing line without reading the files. |

See [Compiler Configuration](./Compiler%20Configuration.md) for the config file form.

### Programmatic use

`Compiler.compileWithSourceMap()` and `Compiler.exportWithSourceMap()` return the program and
its map without writing files:

```ts
import { Compiler, createMemoryCompilerIoApi, defaultOptions, COMPILER_VERSION } from "@harmoniclabs/pebble";

const compiler = new Compiler( io, { ...defaultOptions, compilerVersion: COMPILER_VERSION } );
const { bytes, sourceMap } = await compiler.compileWithSourceMap({ entry: "src/index.pebble", root: "." });
```

The map format belongs to `@harmoniclabs/plutus-machine` (version 1); its README documents every
field. The parts that matter when reading a failure:

| Field        | Contents                                                                     |
|--------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `sources`    | the files of the project, paths relative to the root                          |
| `mappings`   | one `[ term, source, startLine, startColumn, endLine, endColumn ]` per term    |
| `functions`  | where each function body starts, so a stack can name the open calls           |
| `asserts`    | the term that computes each assert's condition, and the assert's range        |
| `traces`     | the traces the compiler removed from the script (below)                       |
| `tracePoints`| where each of those traces would have run                                     |

`locateFailure`, `formatFailure` and `evaluateWithSourceMap` in `@harmoniclabs/plutus-machine`
turn a map and a failed evaluation into a location and a stack.

## Traces are removed from the script and kept in the map

`removeTraces` removes `trace` statements and the messages of `assert` and `fail` from the
compiled script. It is `true` in the production options — the default for `pebble compile`,
`pebble export` and `pebble test`.

```json
{
  "compilerVersion": "^0.6.0",
  "removeTraces": false
}
```

- A script compiled with `removeTraces` is smaller and cheaper, and has a **new hash**: the
  UPLC-CAPE `two_party_escrow` (11 assert messages) goes from 1354 to 853 bytes.
- The traces are removed **before** anything is optimized, so the program is byte for byte the
  one the source without them compiles to: a value computed only for a trace is not computed,
  and the optimizer may drop a branch that only failed with a message.
- The **failures stay**: an `assert` that fails still fails, with the error of a script that
  had no message.
- The map keeps them, so tools print them back where they would have run, in order with the
  traces the program kept: `pebble test`, `pebble debug`, buildooor, and
  `evaluateWithSourceMap`.
- `pebble compile` and `pebble export` report how many traces they removed, and name the ones
  the optimizer left no place for (code it removed because it never runs):

  ```text
  compiled program written to ./out/out.flat
  source map written to ./out/out.flat.map
  3 traces removed (removeTraces); the source map keeps them
  ```

A message computed from values (`trace acc;`, `assert x > 10 else "x is " + x.show();`) is
computed on the side, from the values the program holds at that point — `trace acc;` after a
loop prints the value the loop computed. When the optimizer removed the value the message reads
(a helper inlined with its argument), the log says so:
`<x: not computed by the stripped script>`.

Set `removeTraces: false` to keep the traces inside the script — useful when the script is
inspected by a node or a tool that does not read source maps. The examples in the compiler
repository do.

## `pebble test` prints where a test failed

A failing test reports the location of the failure and the open calls, innermost first:

```text
src/index.test.pebble
  FAIL  small_input  [cpu: 413390, mem: 2401]
        trace: x must be greater than 10
        error: explicit error from uplc
        at check (src/index.pebble:2:5)
        at entry (src/index.pebble:7:15)
        at test small_input (src/index.test.pebble:4:15)
  PASS  big_input  [cpu: 588676, mem: 2604]

Tests: 1 passed, 1 failed, 0 skipped, 2 total
```

`--json` gains `location` and `stack` next to `error`; `TestIterationResult.error` gains the same
two fields. See [Testing](./Testing.md).

The locations are right where optimizations would mislead a simpler resolver: two asserts merged
into one `error` report the one whose condition was false; an `if( x ) fail;` whose `error`
branch is pruned reports the `if`; a helper the optimizer copied into its caller still gets its
own frame, pointing at the call.

## `pebble debug` — one evaluation, statement by statement

`pebble debug` records **one** evaluation and prints it in source order: a test (`--test <name>`)
or a script evaluation buildooor saved (`--eval <file>`).

```bash
pebble debug --test small_input
```

```text
test small_input  src/index.test.pebble: 3 steps, failed at step 3

test small_input  src/index.test.pebble
  #1    4  const r = entry( 5 )                              r = <not evaluated>
           → entry  src/index.pebble
  #2    7    const v = check( x )                            v = <not evaluated>
             → check  src/index.pebble
  #3    2      assert x > 10 else "x must be greater than 10";  <- failed
                 x = 5
failed: explicit error from uplc (cpu 413390, mem 2401)
trace: x must be greater than 10
```

Each line is a statement; the calls it makes are printed under it, indented; the failing
statement lists every variable in scope.

| Option               | Meaning                                                                     |
|----------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--test <name>`      | debug the test with this name, or part of it, among the tests of `[path]`     |
| `--eval <file>`      | replay a saved script evaluation (buildooor's `saveFailedEvaluations`)        |
| `--step <n>`         | print step `n` in full: the open calls, every variable with its whole value   |
| `--all`              | list the variables in scope at every step                                     |
| `--json`             | emit the steps, the variables and the result as JSON                          |
| `--max-states <n>`   | record at most `n` machine states (default `2000000`)                         |
| `--property-runs <n>`| iterations of a property test to look for a failure in (default `100`)        |
| `--seed <int>`       | seed for the property-test PRNG (default `0`)                                 |
| `-c, --config <path>`| the config file (default `./pebble.config.json`)                              |

It exits 0 whenever the evaluation could be shown, passed or failed: a failing run is a
successful debug.

`--step` prints one step with the whole value of every variable:

```text
step 2 of 3
  src/index.pebble:7:5  const v = check( x )
stack:
  entry  src/index.pebble:7:5  const v = check( x )
  test small_input  src/index.test.pebble:4:5  const r = entry( 5 )
declares:
  v: int = <not evaluated>
variables:
  x: int = 5
budget of the statement: cpu 32000, mem 200
```

### What the steps are

The steps follow the **source**, not the machine: the compiled program computes a `const` where
it is used, merges asserts and hoists what does not depend on the call.

- Evaluation is pure, so each call lists the statements whose terms ran, sorted as written.
- A call the optimizer computed ahead of its caller still shows under the statement that makes
  it.
- A loop runs one frame per iteration: condition, body, update.
- A failing run ends at the statement that failed.

Variables carry their source names and types and the value they have **at that statement**
(after reassignments, in that iteration), decoded with the type: `TxOutRef{ id: #…, index: 0 }`,
`Some{ value: 7 }`, `true` for a boolean read from data. Two markers say why a value is missing:

| Marker            | Meaning                                                                |
|-------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `<not evaluated>` | the run never needed the value                                          |
| `<optimized out>` | the compiler removed the variable                                       |

The debug information stays in memory: `out.flat.map` does not change, and neither does the
program.

### Programmatic use

```ts
// the program and its map, plus the debug table: what `pebble debug` compiles with
const { bytes, sourceMap, debugTable } = await compiler.compileWithDebugInfo();

// a test of the project, by name or by part of it
const { test, run } = await compiler.debugTest({
    entry: "src/index.test.pebble",
    root: ".",
    name: "small_input",
    maxStates: 2000000,   // optional
});

// a saved evaluation: `term` is the script as the transaction carried it
const saved = await compiler.debugScript({ term: savedEvaluationTerm( json ), costModel, budget });
```

`debugTest` also takes `propertyIterations` and `seed` for a property test. `debugScript` throws
when the term is not the program the project compiles to (it compares the map's `programHash`).

A `DebugRun` holds `steps` and `frames`, `failedStep`, `variablesAt( step )`,
`declaredAt( step )`, `stackAt( step )`, and `next( step, mode )` / `prev( step, mode )` with
`mode` one of `"into"`, `"over"`, `"out"` — the same walk `pebble debug` prints.
`formatDebugRun`, `formatDebugStep`, `debugRunToJson`, `decodeValue` and `formatValue` format
it.

## Debugging a failed transaction: buildooor

`@harmoniclabs/buildooor` 0.3.0 reads the same maps, so a script that fails while a transaction
is built reports where it failed in the source:

```text
script '470f…' consumed with Spend redeemer and index '0'
failed at src/index.pebble:50:13
    at TwoPartyEscrow (src/index.pebble:50:13)
```

Give the builder the maps and, optionally, a directory where it saves every failed evaluation:

```ts
const txBuilder = new TxBuilder( protocolParameters, genesisInfos, {
    sourceMaps: [ readFileSync( "escrow/out/out.flat.map", "utf8" ) ],
    saveFailedEvaluations: "./failed",
});
```

Each saved file holds the script as the transaction carries it, its arguments, the cost model and
the budget, so it can be replayed from the Pebble project:

```bash
pebble debug --eval ./failed/spend-0-470f22571c405a0a.json
```

buildooor's `docs/SOURCE_MAPS.md` documents the options, the error shape and the file format.

## See also

- [CLI](./CLI.md) — every command and flag, including `pebble debug` and the REPL
- [Testing](./Testing.md) — writing and running tests
- [Compiler Configuration](./Compiler%20Configuration.md) — `sourceMap`, `sourceMapContent`, `removeTraces`
- [Diagnostics](./reference/Diagnostics.md) — warnings about values that are never computed


=== onchain/Prelude/Array.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 7
sidebar_label: Array<T>
---

# `Array<T>`

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

A fixed-size, indexed container. Built from a `List<T>` via [`std.array.fromList`](../Standard%20Library/std.array.mdx) and consumed via `at(i)` or the index operator.

`Array<T>` is **not** the right answer to "I need fast indexed reads on a `List<T>`". The on-chain cost model bills [`List<T>` indexing](./List.mdx) as effectively constant for practical indices, and `std.array.fromList` itself is O(n) in the list length — so the conversion almost always costs more than the reads you were optimising. See [Cost and Complexity](../reference/Cost%20and%20Complexity.md) for the measured numbers.

Reach for `Array<T>` only when:
- You receive one from elsewhere (an external API, a builtin) and need to read it.
- You're doing many indexed reads against a buffer that you'll keep across many call sites and the amortised conversion is genuinely cheap.

For sequential traversal (`map`, `foldl`, `filter`, ...), use `List<T>` directly.

import RunnableExample from '@site/src/components/RunnableExample';

<RunnableExample
initialCode={`const xs: Array<int> = std.array.fromList([10, 20, 30, 40]);\n\nassert std.array.length(xs) == 4 else "wrong length";\nassert std.array.at(xs, 2)  == 30 else "at(2) wrong";`}
height="240px"
/>

## Methods

`Array<T>` has **no methods**: every operation is a function of
[`std.array`](../Standard%20Library/std.array.mdx).

| Function                                   | Description                                                                |
|--------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `std.array.length(xs): int`                | Number of elements.                                                        |
| `std.array.at(xs, i): int`                 | Element at index `i`. Fails on out-of-bounds.                              |
| `std.array.fromList(xs): Array<T>`         | Build an array from a list. O(n).                                          |

### Example
```ts
function at(): bool {
    const xs: Array<int> = std.array.fromList([10, 20, 30]);

    const n: int = std.array.length( xs );   // 3
    const v: int = std.array.at( xs, 1 );    // 20
    assert n == 3 && v == 20;
    return true;
}
```

`xs.length()` and `xs.at(1)` are **not** methods of `Array<T>`: they are error 2339.

## Indexing

`xs[i]` is not available on an `Array<T>` (error 267, "This expression cannot be indexed"): index
it with `std.array.at( xs, i )`. On a `List<T>`, `xs[i]` is the indexed read and is cheap.

## Constructing

`Array<T>` has no literal form. Build one from a list:

```ts
const xs: Array<int> = std.array.fromList([1, 2, 3]);
```

## See also

- [`std.array`](../Standard%20Library/std.array.mdx) — function-call surface
- [`List<T>`](./List.mdx) — what most pipelines operate on. Indexed reads on a list are already cheap; don't convert unless you have a specific reason
- [Cost and Complexity](../reference/Cost%20and%20Complexity.md) — measured numbers for list-vs-array access


=== onchain/Prelude/Boolean.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 4
sidebar_label: bool
---

# `bool`

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

Logical truth value: `true` or `false`. Maps to Plutus Core `Bool`.

```ts
const signed: bool = tx.requiredSigners.includes(ownerHash);

if( signed && tx.outputs.length() > 0 ) {
    trace("OK");
} else {
    fail "Unauthorized";
}
```

## Literals

`true`, `false`.

## Operators

| Category    | Operators                                                                |
|-------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Logical     | `&&` (short-circuit AND), `\|\|` (short-circuit OR), `!` (NOT)           |
| Equality    | `==`, `!=`                                                               |

:::tip Short-circuit vs strict
`&&` and `\|\|` are short-circuit: the right operand is only evaluated if the left doesn't decide the result. If you need strict evaluation (rare — usually for higher-order use), see [`std.boolean.strictAnd`](../Standard%20Library/std.boolean.mdx) and `strictOr`.
:::

## Methods

`bool` has no method-call surface. Use operators or the [`std.boolean`](../Standard%20Library/std.boolean.mdx) namespace.

## On-chain encoding

A `bool` converted to `data` — `.toData()`, a field of a datum, a redeemer — is `Constr 0 []` for
`false` and `Constr 1 []` for `true`.

```ts
function encoding(): bool {
    using { constrData } = std.builtins;
    assert true.toData()  == constrData( 1, [] );
    assert false.toData() == constrData( 0, [] );
    return true;
}
```

| value   | `data`        | off-chain (`@harmoniclabs/plutus-data`) |
|---------|---------------|------------------------------------------|
| `false` | `Constr 0 []` | `new DataConstr( 0, [] )`                |
| `true`  | `Constr 1 []` | `new DataConstr( 1, [] )`                |

:::caution breaking change in 0.6.0
Up to 0.5.0 the two were the other way round. Consequences of the fix:

- A contract with a `boolean` in a datum, a redeemer, or any value it serialises or compares as
  data has a **new hash**, and reads the booleans of UTxOs created for the old script inverted.
  Contracts with no boolean crossing data are unchanged, byte for byte.
- A boolean of the ledger's is read correctly: `tx.validityInterval.from.isInclusive` is `true` for
  a closed bound (`false` before). The `std.interval` helpers read the constructor themselves and
  were already right.
- A datum or redeemer built off-chain from the encoding above is now read as written.
:::

## See also

- [`std.boolean`](../Standard%20Library/std.boolean.mdx) — function-call surface
- [`std.builtins`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx#polymorphic-intrinsics) — `ifThenElse<T>` is the strict polymorphic conditional


=== onchain/Prelude/Bytes.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 2
sidebar_label: bytes
---

# `bytes`

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

Raw byte string. Maps to Plutus Core `ByteString`. Used for hashes, policy IDs, token names, signatures, and anything else that's "just bytes on the wire".

import RunnableExample from '@site/src/components/RunnableExample';

<RunnableExample
initialCode={`const policy:    bytes = #deadbeef;\nconst tokenName: bytes = #4d79546f6b656e;\n\nassert std.bytes.length(policy) == 4         else "wrong width";\nassert std.bytes.slice(1, 2, policy) == #adbe else "slice off";\nassert tokenName == #4d79546f6b656e            else "utf-8 off";`}
height="240px"
/>

## Literals

| Form                | Example                | Notes                                                       |
|---------------------|------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| Hex literal         | `#1a2b3c`              | Each pair of hex digits is one byte. Case-insensitive.      |
| Empty               | `#""`                  | Zero-length byte string.                                    |
| Double-quoted       | `"MyToken"`            | Its UTF-8 bytes — a `bytes` literal, not a `string`.        |

## Operators

| Category      | Operators                            |
|---------------|--------------------------------------|
| Equality      | `==`, `!=`                           |
| Concatenation | `+` (`#dead + #beef`), and `+=`      |
| Ordering      | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` (lexicographic) |

`+` concatenates two byte strings (and two string literals, which are byte strings). `+=` adds
whatever `+` adds, so `acc += #ff;` on a `bytes` variable works — before 0.6.0 `+=` was ints only.

## Methods

| Method                                                | Description                                                                |
|-------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `length(): int`                                       | Number of bytes.                                                            |
| `slice(start: int, len: int): bytes`                  | `len`-byte sub-string starting at `start`. Clips on out-of-range.           |
| `prepend(byteVal: int): bytes`                        | Returns a new byte string with `byteVal` (0–255) prepended.                 |
| `concat(other: bytes): bytes`                         | Concatenate; same as `a + other`.                                           |
| `indexAt(i: int): int`                                | Byte at index `i` as `0–255`. Fails on out-of-range.                        |
| `equals(other: bytes): bool`                          | Same as `==`.                                                               |
| `lessThan(other: bytes): bool`                        | Same as `<`.                                                                |
| `lessThanEquals(other: bytes): bool`                  | Same as `<=`.                                                               |
| `greaterThan(other: bytes): bool`                     | Same as `>`.                                                                |
| `greaterThanEquals(other: bytes): bool`               | Same as `>=`.                                                               |
| `toInt(): int`                                        | Parse as big-endian unsigned integer.                                       |

### Examples (one per method)
```ts
const policy: bytes = #deadbeef;

const n:    int   = policy.length();                       // 4
const sub:  bytes = policy.slice(1, 2);                    // #adbe
const pre:  bytes = policy.prepend(0xff);                  // #ffdeadbeef
const cat:  bytes = #dead.concat(#beef);                   // #deadbeef
const at:   int   = policy.indexAt(0);                     // 222 (0xde)
const eq:   bool  = policy.equals(#deadbeef);              // true
const lt:   bool  = #ab.lessThan(#cd);                     // true
const le:   bool  = #ab.lessThanEquals(#ab);               // true
const gt:   bool  = #cd.greaterThan(#ab);                  // true
const ge:   bool  = #ab.greaterThanEquals(#ab);            // true
const i:    int   = #04d2.toInt();                         // 1234
```

## Type aliases

The standard library defines several `bytes` aliases for clarity at usage sites:

| Alias          | Width | Used for                                  |
|----------------|-------|-------------------------------------------|
| `Hash28`       | 28    | Generic 224-bit hashes.                   |
| `Hash32`       | 32    | Generic 256-bit hashes.                   |
| `PubKeyHash`   | 28    | Blake2b-224 of a payment public key.      |
| `ScriptHash`   | 28    | Blake2b-224 of a serialized script.       |
| `TxHash`       | 32    | Blake2b-256 of a serialized transaction.  |
| `PolicyId`     | 28    | The script hash of a minting policy.      |
| `TokenName`    | 0–32  | An asset name within a policy.            |

These are aliases, not nominal types — you can freely pass a `bytes` where any of them is expected and vice versa.

## See also

- [`std.bytes`](../Standard%20Library/std.bytes.mdx) — function-call surface
- [`std.crypto`](../Standard%20Library/std.crypto.mdx) — hash functions produce `bytes`
- [`std.builtins`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx) — bitwise operations and `consByteString`, `replicateByte`, etc.


=== onchain/Prelude/Data.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 5
sidebar_label: data
---

# `data`

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

The Plutus Core `Data` type: a serialization format that every on-chain type can be encoded into and decoded from. Datums, redeemers, and the script context all flow through `data` at the system boundary.

You rarely write `data` directly; the compiler does it for you whenever you use `.toData()` or pattern-match a datum. Reach for raw `data` only when you need to construct or inspect the CBOR shape yourself.

`data` has five constructors (CBOR major types in parentheses):

| Constructor | Shape                                  | Builtin builder                                 |
|-------------|----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| Constr      | `(index: int, fields: List<data>)`     | [`std.builtins.constrData`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx) |
| Map         | `LinearMap<data, data>`                | [`std.builtins.mapData`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx)   |
| List        | `List<data>`                           | [`std.builtins.listData`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx)  |
| I (integer) | `int`                                  | [`std.builtins.iData`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx)     |
| B (bytes)   | `bytes`                                | [`std.builtins.bData`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx)     |

## Operators

| Category | Operators       |
|----------|-----------------|
| Equality | `==`, `!=`      |

Equality is structural CBOR equality, implemented by `equalsData`.

## Working with `data`

```ts
function shape( d: data ): int {
    using { constrData, unConstrData, iData, bData } = std.builtins;

    // Build:
    const built: data = constrData(0, [iData(42), bData(#cafe)]);

    // Destructure a constructor:
    const RawConstr{ index, fields } = unConstrData( d );

    if( index == 0 ) { trace("Some"); }
    else { fail "unknown constructor"; }

    return index;
}
```

`unConstrData` returns a `RawConstr` with two fields, `index: int` and `fields: List<data>`; both
can be destructured in one `const`, as above, and `fields` can be destructured further. *Since
0.6.0* the destructuring works with one property, without the type name, and inside a map entry
(`value: RawConstr{ index }`).

`using { … } = std.builtins;` binds the names in the **block** it appears in — here, the function
body. Put it inside the function or method that uses them; a `using` at file scope is accepted by
the parser but does not bring names into a function's body.

### `Optional<T>.toData()`

An `Optional<T>` has `.toData()` like every other encodable type: `Some{ value: v }` is
`Constr 0 [ v ]`, `None{}` is `Constr 1 []` — the encoding a struct field of that type has.

```ts
function encoding(): bool {
    using { constrData, iData } = std.builtins;
    const some: Optional<int> = Some{ value: 7 };
    const none: Optional<int> = undefined;
    assert some.toData() == constrData( 0, [ iData( 7 ) ] );
    assert none.toData() == constrData( 1, [] );
    return true;
}
```

For most use cases prefer the `.toData()` method (via the [`ToData`](../Builtin%20Interfaces.md#todata) interface) and pattern-matching on the typed value, rather than touching raw `data`.

## See also

- [`std.builtins`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx) — `data` constructors and destructors, `serialiseData`, `equalsData`
- [`std.data`](../Standard%20Library/std.data.mdx) — `string ↔ data` helpers
- [`ToData`](../Builtin%20Interfaces.md#todata) — auto-derived `.toData()` for every encodable type
- [`LinearMap<K, V>`](./LinearMap.mdx), [`List<T>`](./List.mdx) — the containers `data` is built from


=== onchain/Prelude/Int.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 1
sidebar_label: int

# `int`

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

Arbitrary-precision signed integer. Maps to Plutus Core's `Integer`. Does not overflow.

import RunnableExample from '@site/src/components/RunnableExample';

<RunnableExample
initialCode={`const supply: int = 1_000_000;\nlet   spent:  int = 500;\n\nconst left = supply - spent;\nassert left >= 0       else "underflow";\nassert left == 999_500 else "math off";`}
height="220px"
/>

## Literals

| Form                | Example                | Notes                                       |
|---------------------|------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Decimal             | `42`, `-7`, `0`        | The default form.                           |
| Underscore separator| `1_000_000`            | Cosmetic; ignored at parse time.            |
| Hexadecimal         | `0xCAFE`               | Case-insensitive after the `0x`.            |

## Operators

| Category    | Operators                                                                |
|-------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Arithmetic  | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` (floor division), `%` (floor modulo)                 |
| Comparison  | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==`, `!=`                                         |
| Unary       | `-` (negation)                                                           |

:::note Division semantics
`/` and `%` round toward **negative infinity** (matching `std.int.divide` / `std.int.mod`). For C-style truncated division (toward zero), use [`std.int.quotient`](../Standard%20Library/std.int.mdx) / [`std.int.remainder`](../Standard%20Library/std.int.mdx).
:::

## Methods

`int` has no method-call surface. All operations are via operators or the [`std.int`](../Standard%20Library/std.int.mdx) namespace.

Common idioms:

| Want…                              | Use                                                                       |
|------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Modular exponentiation             | [`std.builtins.expModInteger(base, exp, m)`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx) |
| `int → bytes` (smallest fit)       | [`std.bytes.fromInt(n)`](../Standard%20Library/std.bytes.mdx)             |
| `int → bytes` (fixed width)        | [`std.builtins.integerToByteString(true, size, n)`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx) |
| `int → bool`                       | [`std.int.toBoolean(n)`](../Standard%20Library/std.int.mdx)               |
| Encoded as `data`                  | `n.toData()` ([`ToData`](../Builtin%20Interfaces.md#todata)) — uses `iData` |

## See also

- [`std.int`](../Standard%20Library/std.int.mdx) — function-call surface
- [`bytes`](./Bytes.mdx) — conversion target
- [`ToData`](../Builtin%20Interfaces.md#todata) — auto-derived `.toData()`


=== onchain/Prelude/LinearMap.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 8
sidebar_label: LinearMap<K, V>
---

# `LinearMap<K, V>`

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

An association list — Cardano's on-chain "map". Structurally a `List` of `(K, V)` entries. Lookups are O(n); choose it because the underlying Plutus representation is what the chain speaks, not because it's fast.

```ts
const m: LinearMap<bytes, int> = { #01: 10, #02: 20 };

function first( m: LinearMap<bytes, int> ): int {
    match m.lookup(#01) {
        when Some{ value: amount }: return amount
        when None{}: fail "missing"
    }
}
```

## Literals

```ts
const empty: LinearMap<bytes, int> = {};
const m: LinearMap<bytes, int> = { #01: 10, #02: 20 };
```

- The key/value types come from the expected type, or — without one — from the **first entry**.
- A key is any expression, **except a bare identifier**: `{ a: 1 }` is a struct's field, so a
  variable used as a key is written `{ (a): 1 }` (error 30212 otherwise).
- Entries keep their order, **duplicate keys included**.
- A map literal where another type is expected is error 30211.

```ts
function keyed( a: bytes ): LinearMap<bytes, int> {
    const m: LinearMap<bytes, int> = { #01: 10, (a): 20, #01: 30 };
    assert m.length() == 3;      // three entries: #01 appears twice
    return m;
}
```

## In type position

Since `0.3.6`, `LinearMap<K, V>` is a first-class type everywhere a type can
appear — struct fields, `type` alias targets, annotations:

```ts
// e.g. CIP-68 metadata
struct RootNft {
    metadata: LinearMap<bytes, bytes>,
    version: int,
    extra: data
}
```

Entries are `data`-encoded on-chain regardless of `K`/`V`; typed maps
convert at the boundaries automatically. In particular `lookup` encodes a
typed key for the underlying `equalsData` comparison (since `0.3.7`), so
`dd.metadata.lookup( #6d6564696154797065 )` works exactly like a lookup on
a `LinearMap<data, data>` obtained from
[`unMapData`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx#data-destructors).

## Methods

| Method                                                                                     | Description                                                                |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `length(): int`                                                                            | Number of entries. O(n).                                                   |
| `isEmpty(): bool`                                                                          | True iff there are no entries.                                             |
| `head(): LinearMapEntry<K, V>`                                                             | First `(K, V)` pair. Fails on empty.                                       |
| `tail(): LinearMap<K, V>`                                                                  | Map without its first entry. Fails on empty.                               |
| `reverse(): LinearMap<K, V>`                                                               | The same entries, last first.                                              |
| `lookup(k: K): Optional<V>`                                                                | First value bound to `k`, wrapped in `Some`, or `None`.                    |
| `find(p: (entry) => bool): Optional<LinearMapEntry<K, V>>`                                 | First entry satisfying `p`.                                                |
| `filter(p: (entry) => bool): LinearMap<K, V>`                                              | The entries satisfying `p`.                                                |
| `map(f: (entry) => T): List<T>`                                                            | One value per entry.                                                       |
| `every(p: (entry) => bool): bool`                                                          | True iff `p` holds for every entry.                                        |
| `some(p: (entry) => bool): bool`                                                           | True iff `p` holds for at least one entry.                                 |
| `includes(entry): bool`                                                                    | Whether this exact entry is in the map.                                    |
| `prepend(k: K, v: V): LinearMap<K, V>` (requires `K: ToData`, `V: ToData`)                 | Add `(k, v)` at the front. Both type parameters must implement `ToData`.   |

`reverse`, `find` and `includes` were accepted and had no backend before 0.6.0; `map.find( … )`
failed in the backend.

:::note Duplicate keys
`LinearMap` allows duplicates. `lookup` returns the **first** match. To enforce uniqueness, do so at insertion or de-duplicate before lookup.
:::

### Examples (one per method)
```ts
function methods( m: LinearMap<bytes, int> ): bool {
    const n:   int                 = m.length();                    // 2
    const e:   bool                = m.isEmpty();                   // false
    const h                        = m.head();                      // (#01, 10)
    const t:   LinearMap<bytes, int> = m.tail();                    // { #02: 20 }
    const r:   LinearMap<bytes, int> = m.reverse();                 // { #02: 20, #01: 10 }
    const got: Optional<int>       = m.lookup(#02);                 // Some{ value: 20 }
    const f                        = m.find(( en ) => en.value == 20 );
    const fl:  LinearMap<bytes, int> = m.filter(( en ) => en.value > 15 );
    const vs:  List<int>           = m.map(( en ) => en.value );
    const m2:  LinearMap<bytes, int> = m.prepend(#03, 30);          // { #03:30, #01:10, #02:20 }
    assert m.includes( h );
    return m.every(( en ) => en.value > 0 ) && m.some(( en ) => en.value == 20 );
}
```

## The entry type

`head()`, `find()` and a `for...of` loop give an entry: a value with two fields.

| Field    | Type | Description       |
|----------|------|-------------------|
| `key`    | `K`  | The key.          |
| `value`  | `V`  | The value.        |

Access them by field or by **destructuring**:

```ts
function keys( m: LinearMap<bytes, int> ): List<bytes> {
    const { key, value } = m.head();
    trace( key );
    trace( value );
    return m.map(( entry ) => entry.key );
}
```

The entry type has no name to write in an annotation: let it be inferred (`const h = m.head();`),
or destructure it.

## Iteration

`LinearMap<K, V>` is structurally a list, so anything that works on a list works here. To iterate, use `for...of` or list helpers:

```ts
function total( m: LinearMap<bytes, int> ): int {
    let sum: int = 0;
    for( const entry of m ) {
        const { key, value } = entry;
        trace(key);
        sum += value;
    }
    return sum;
}
```

## See also

- [`std.linearMap`](../Standard%20Library/std.linearMap.mdx) — function-call surface
- [`List<T>`](./List.mdx) — structural relative
- [`std.builtins`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx#data-destructors) — `mapData` / `unMapData`


=== onchain/Prelude/List.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 6
sidebar_label: List<T>
---

# `List<T>`

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

A singly-linked list of elements of type `T`. Maps to Plutus Core's built-in list.

Despite being a cons list at the interpreter level, **indexed access `xs[i]` is essentially free in the on-chain cost model**: it lowers to `headList (dropList i xs)`, and `dropList` is billed by the bit-width of `i` (constant for any practical index), not by how many cons cells get walked. So unlike with arrays in other languages, you don't need to convert to [`Array<T>`](./Array.mdx) for cheap indexed reads — see [Cost and Complexity](../reference/Cost%20and%20Complexity.md) for the measured numbers.

import RunnableExample from '@site/src/components/RunnableExample';

<RunnableExample
initialCode={`const xs: List<int> = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];\n\nconst total = std.list.foldl((acc, n) => acc + n, 0, xs);\nconst evens = std.list.filter((n) => n % 2 == 0, xs);\n\nassert total == 15                    else "sum wrong";\nassert std.list.length(evens) == 2    else "filter wrong";`}
height="280px"
/>

## Literals

```ts
const empty: List<int> = [];
const xs: List<int>    = [1, 2, 3];
```

The element type is inferred from context (or from the first element if obvious).

## Methods

| Method                                                       | Description                                                                |
|--------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `length(): int`                                              | Element count. Walks the spine; O(n) in actual work, charged O(n) by the cost model. |
| `isEmpty(): bool`                                            | True if the list has zero elements.                                       |
| `head(): T`                                                  | First element. Fails on empty.                                             |
| `tail(): List<T>`                                            | Everything after the head. Fails on empty.                                 |
| `reverse(): List<T>`                                         | The same elements, last first.                                             |
| `prepend(x: T): List<T>`                                     | New list with `x` at the front.                                            |
| `map<A>(f: (T) -> A): List<A>`                               | Transform every element. Method-only — there's no `std.list.map`.          |
| `filter(p: (T) -> bool): List<T>`                            | Keep only elements satisfying `p`.                                         |
| `some(p: (T) -> bool): bool`                                 | True if any element satisfies `p`. Short-circuits.                        |
| `every(p: (T) -> bool): bool`                                | True if all elements satisfy `p`. Short-circuits.                         |
| `includes(x: T): bool`                                       | True if `x` is an element of the list.                                     |
| `find(p: (T) -> bool): Optional<T>`                          | First match wrapped in `Some`, or `None`.                                  |
| `show(): bytes`                                              | The list as text.                                                          |

`drop`, `foldl`, `foldr`, `at`, `concat` and `equals` are functions of
[`std.list`](../Standard%20Library/std.list.mdx), not methods: `std.list.drop(2, xs)`,
`std.list.foldl((acc, n) => acc + n, 0, xs)`. `reverse` was accepted and had no backend before
0.6.0.

### Examples (one per method)
```ts
function methods( xs: List<int> ): bool {
    const n:    int           = xs.length();                       // 5
    const e:    bool          = xs.isEmpty();                      // false
    const h:    int           = xs.head();                         // 1
    const t:    List<int>     = xs.tail();                         // [2,3,4,5]
    const r:    List<int>     = xs.reverse();                      // [5,4,3,2,1]
    const ys:   List<int>     = xs.prepend(0);                     // [0,1,2,3,4,5]
    const dbl:  List<int>     = xs.map((n) => n * 2);              // [2,4,6,8,10]
    const ev:   List<int>     = xs.filter((n) => n % 2 == 0);      // [2,4]
    const any:  bool          = xs.some((n) => n > 4);             // true
    const all:  bool          = xs.every((n) => n > 0);            // true
    const has:  bool          = xs.includes(3);                    // true
    const got:  Optional<int> = xs.find((n) => n == 3);            // Some{ value: 3 }
    const sum:  int           = std.list.foldl((acc, a) => acc + a, 0, xs);  // 15
    assert xs == xs;                                               // element-wise, when `T` has equality
    return true;
}
```

### Pipeline example
```ts
struct Input { policy: bytes, name: bytes, amount: int }

function total( inputs: List<Input>, myPolicy: bytes ): int {
    return std.list.foldl(
        ( acc, i ) => acc + i.amount,
        0,
        inputs.filter((i) => i.policy == myPolicy)
    );
}
```

## Indexing

`xs[i]` is sugar for accessing the i-th element. It lowers to `headList(dropList(i, xs))`. The interpreter does O(i) work walking the spine, but the **on-chain cost model bills `dropList` by the bit-width of `i`**, so for any practical index the charged cost is essentially constant. **Don't convert to `Array<T>` just for indexed reads** — `std.array.fromList` itself is linear in the list length, and that conversion is almost always more expensive than however many list-indexing reads you were trying to optimise. Reserve the conversion for scenarios where you genuinely need many random-access reads against the *same* compact buffer.

See [Cost and Complexity](../reference/Cost%20and%20Complexity.md) for the measured numbers.

## Operators

| Category | Operators                                            |
|----------|------------------------------------------------------|
| Equality | `==`, `!=` (when `T` implements equality)            |

`List<T>` has no equality when `T` has none (a function, a BLS12-381 element, an `Array`, a runtime
struct): `==` on such a list is error 2365 at the operator.

## Element and list types

- `List<Optional<T>>` is a valid type for a variable, a parameter, a literal, and for a list read
  out of a datum and passed to a function. `prepend` works on it.
- A `List<T>` whose `T` is a **runtime struct** is refused where it is written (error 30213): no
  UPLC list holds a constructor term. Declare the struct `data`, or keep such values in a
  recursive runtime struct.
- A cast between two lists, `std.builtins.unListData( d ) as List<Asset>`, gives the elements of a
  list read off some data their type; a list of data cast to a list of integers decodes each
  element. A list of integers as a list of byte strings is refused by the checker.

## See also

- [`std.list`](../Standard%20Library/std.list.mdx) — function-call surface
- [`Array<T>`](./Array.mdx) — random-access counterpart
- [`LinearMap<K, V>`](./LinearMap.mdx) — structurally a `List<LinearMapEntry<K, V>>`
- [`std.builtins`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx#polymorphic-intrinsics) — `mkCons`, `headList`, `tailList`, `nullList`, `chooseList`


=== onchain/Prelude/Optional.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 9
sidebar_label: Optional<T>
---

# `Optional<T>`

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

A value that may be absent. Two constructors:

| Constructor        | Payload    | Meaning                |
|--------------------|------------|------------------------|
| `Some{ value: T }` | `value: T` | The value is present.  |
| `None{}`           | —          | The value is absent.   |

```ts
const maybe: Optional<int> = Some{ value: 42 };
const nothing: Optional<int> = undefined;
```

`Optional` is returned by every "lookup-shaped" operation in the standard library:
[`List.find`](./List.mdx), [`LinearMap.lookup`](./LinearMap.mdx), and so on.

## Constructing

`Some{ value: v }` is a **value**: it can be assigned, returned, passed and compared.

```ts
function made(): Optional<int> {
    return Some{ value: 42 };
}
```

The empty optional is written `undefined` or `None{}`; the two are the same value.

```ts
const absent: Optional<int> = undefined;
const alsoAbsent: Optional<int> = None{};
assert absent == alsoAbsent;
```

`undefined` needs an `Optional` type annotation, since nothing else says what it is empty *of*.
`None{}` needs one too when it is not in a position the compiler can infer from.

## One type, two representations

*Since 0.6.0* an `Optional<T>` is **one type**, wherever it comes from. An `Optional` read out of a
datum and one made in a function are different values at run time — a data-encoded `Constr` and a
sum-of-products tag — and the compiler converts between them where the value crosses from one to
the other: `return`, an annotated `const` or `let`, an assignment, the arms of `?:` and `case`,
struct fields, list elements, and the operands of `==`.

Before 0.6.0 that conversion existed for call arguments only, so these were refused
(`Type 'Optional<int>' is not assignable to type 'Optional<int>'`) or failed in the backend.

## Encoding

`.toData()` gives the encoding a struct field of this type has: `Constr 0 [ v ]` for
`Some{ value: v }`, `Constr 1 []` for the empty optional.

```ts
function encoding(): bool {
    using { constrData, iData } = std.builtins;
    const some: Optional<int> = Some{ value: 7 };
    const none: Optional<int> = undefined;
    assert some.toData() == constrData( 0, [ iData( 7 ) ] );
    assert none.toData() == constrData( 1, [] );
    return true;
}
```

## Equality

`==` and `!=` work on any two `Optional`s of the same type, including one read from a datum and one
made in a function, the result of `find` and of `lookup`, and against `undefined`:

```ts
function check( xs: List<int> ): bool {
    assert xs.find(( x ) => x > 1 ) == Some{ value: 2 };
    assert xs.find(( x ) => x > 9 ) == undefined;
    return true;
}
```

## Destructuring with `match`

`match` is the canonical way to consume an `Optional`. Each arm starts with `when`:

```ts
function show( maybe: Optional<int> ): int {
    match maybe {
        when Some{ value }: return value
        when None{}: return 0
    }
}
```

`Some{}` binding no field is a valid pattern: `when Some{}: …` matches any present value.

## Destructuring with `case`

`case` is the expression form. It takes `is` arms and an optional `else`:

```ts
function amountOf( maybe: Optional<int> ): int {
    return case maybe
        is Some{ value } => value
        else 0;
}
```

The `else` arm is type-checked like the others.

## Narrowing by `is`

A variable narrowed by `is` — `if( o is Some )`, a `case` arm, `o is Some ? … : …` — is still a
value of its type: it can be passed to a function, compared, converted to data, and returned from
the arm that narrowed it.

```ts
function keep( o: Optional<int> ): Optional<int> {
    if( o is Some ) { return o; }
    return Some{ value: 0 };
}
```

## Destructuring with `const`

When you know statically that an `Optional` is `Some`, you can destructure directly:

```ts
const Some{ value: x } = maybe;
```

This compiles to an assertion: if `maybe` is `None{}` at runtime, the script fails. Prefer `match`
or `case` when the value can be absent.

## See also

- [`List<T>.find`](./List.mdx), [`LinearMap<K, V>.lookup`](./LinearMap.mdx) — produce `Optional`
- [`data`](./Data.mdx) — `Optional<T>.toData()` and the raw constructors
- [Builtin Values and Literals](../Builtin%20Values%20and%20Literals.md) — pattern-matching syntax


=== onchain/Prelude/String.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 3
sidebar_label: string
---

# `string`

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

UTF-8 text. Maps to Plutus Core `String`. Primarily for logging via `trace` and for `fail` messages. Avoid storing large strings on-chain — every character costs CPU/memory in the script budget.

```ts
const msg: string = std.builtins.decodeUtf8( "Order filled" );
trace(msg);
```

## Literals

A **double-quoted literal is `bytes`**, not `string`: its UTF-8 bytes, with the methods of `bytes`.

| Form          | Example   | Type    | Notes                                            |
|---------------|-----------|---------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Double-quoted | `"hello"` | `bytes` | UTF-8. Same as `#68656c6c6f`.                     |
| Empty         | `""`      | `bytes` | Zero-length byte string.                          |

`trace` and `fail` take either: a quoted literal is accepted where a `string` is expected. Every
other use of a `string` value needs one to exist:

```ts
const s: string = std.builtins.decodeUtf8( "hello" );   // #68656c6c6f, read as text
```

## Operators

| Category      | Operators  |
|---------------|------------|
| Equality      | `==`, `!=` |
| Concatenation | `+`        |

`+` concatenates two `string`s, and `+=` adds whatever `+` adds.

## Methods

A `string` has **one** method:

| Method                  | Description                                                            |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `encodeUtf8(): bytes`   | The UTF-8 bytes. Equivalent to [`std.builtins.encodeUtf8`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx). |

The methods of `bytes` (`length`, `slice`, `indexAt`, …) are **not** methods of `string`: they
compile to byte-string builtins, which fail when the script runs, so they are error 2339. Ask them
of `s.encodeUtf8()`.

To go from `bytes` back to `string`, use [`std.builtins.decodeUtf8`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx) (it fails on invalid UTF-8).

## Examples

```ts
function roundTrip(): bool {
    const greeting: string = std.builtins.decodeUtf8( "hello" );
    const u8:       bytes  = greeting.encodeUtf8();          // #68656c6c6f

    const back: string = std.builtins.decodeUtf8( u8 );      // "hello"
    assert back == greeting;

    const full: string = greeting + std.builtins.decodeUtf8( ", world" );
    assert full == std.builtins.decodeUtf8( "hello, world" );

    let acc: string = greeting;
    acc += std.builtins.decodeUtf8( "!" );
    assert acc.encodeUtf8().length() == 6;
    return true;
}
```

## See also

- [`bytes`](./Bytes.mdx) — what a quoted literal is, and its methods
- [`std.builtins`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx) — `appendString`, `equalsString`, `encodeUtf8`, `decodeUtf8`
- [`std.data`](../Standard%20Library/std.data.mdx) — `strToData` / `strFromData`
- [`Show`](../Builtin%20Interfaces.md#show) — interface every type can implement to produce a `string` representation


=== onchain/Prelude/Value.mdx ===

---
sidebar_position: 10
sidebar_label: Value
---

# `Value`

*Pebble 0.6.0 · all symbols on this page are stable.*

A multi-asset bundle: zero or more `(PolicyId, TokenName) → amount` entries. Maps to Plutus Core's native value type. ADA appears under a special "ada/lovelace" policy.

Every `TxOut.value`, `Tx.mint`, and `Tx.fee` is a `Value`.

```ts
const out = tx.outputs[0];
assert out.value.lovelaces() >= 2_000_000;
assert out.value.amountOf(myPolicy, myToken) == 1;
```

## Methods

| Method                                                              | Description                                                                  |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `amountOf(policy: PolicyId, name: TokenName): int`                  | Amount of `(policy, name)`. `0` if absent.                                   |
| `lovelaces(): int`                                                  | Amount of ADA, in lovelace.                                                  |
| `insert(policy: PolicyId, name: TokenName, amount: int): Value`     | Return a new `Value` with `(policy, name)` set to `amount`. `0` removes.    |
| `union(other: Value): Value`                                        | Asset-wise sum.                                                              |
| `contains(other: Value): bool`                                      | True iff `self ≥ other` for every asset.                                     |
| `scale(k: int): Value`                                              | Multiply every amount by `k`.                                                |
| `toData(): data`                                                    | CBOR-encode. Auto-derived from [`ToData`](../Builtin%20Interfaces.md#todata). |

### Examples (one per method)
```ts
// there is no `mempty`: get an empty Value by zero-scaling any Value in scope
const empty: Value = tx.mint.scale(0);
const v: Value = empty.insert(myPolicy, myToken, 5);

const a:  int   = v.amountOf(myPolicy, myToken);           // 5
const l:  int   = tx.outputs[0].value.lovelaces();         // ADA in lovelace
const v2: Value = v.insert(myPolicy, myToken, 10);         // overwrite -> 10
const u:  Value = v.union(v);                              // 2× v
const ok: bool  = u.contains(v);                           // true
const s:  Value = v.scale(3);                              // 3× v
const d:  data  = v.toData();
```

### Bundled example
```ts
const need = tx.mint.scale(0)
    .insert(myPolicy, myToken, 1)
    .insert(adaPolicy, adaName, 2_000_000);

assert tx.outputs[0].value.contains(need);
```

## Operators

| Category | Operators                                            |
|----------|------------------------------------------------------|
| Equality | `==`, `!=` (structural)                              |

## Building values

There's no `Value` literal (and no `mempty`) — get an empty starting point by zero-scaling any `Value` already in scope (`tx.mint.scale(0)` is the usual choice; containment-style comparisons ignore any zero entries it may keep), then build up with `insert` and `union`, or destructure values out of a `TxOut`. The underlying primitives are in [`std.builtins`](../Standard%20Library/std.builtins.mdx#native-value-operations) (`insertCoin`, `unionValue`, etc.); the friendlier names live in [`std.value`](../Standard%20Library/std.value.mdx).

## See also

- [`std.value`](../Standard%20Library/std.value.mdx) — function-call surface
- [`PolicyId`, `TokenName`](./Bytes.mdx#type-aliases) — the keys into a `Value`
- [`TxOut`](../API/types/Tx/TxOut.md) — the canonical place a `Value` shows up


=== onchain/Standard Library/std.array.mdx ===

sidebar_position: 6
sidebar_label: std.array
